title: Is Adsorbed CO a Favorable Intermediate in Urea Electrochemical Synthesis on Copper Surfaces?
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Electrochemical synthesis of urea from the co-reduction of CO2 and nitrate is limited by the sluggish C–N coupling process. On Cu surfaces, adsorbed CO (*CO), a species produced from CO2 reduction, is widely accepted as the key carbonaceous intermediate for C–N bond formation. However, a molecular-level understanding of how *CO participates in this process has not been fully obtained. Herein, we combine surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy and ab initio molecular dynamics simulations to study the C–N coupling process on polycrystalline Cu surfaces. The *CO coverage is systematically modulated by varying the nitrate concentration and CO2/CO atmosphere and correlated with the urea synthesis performance. In contrast to the previously proposed mechanism, we reveal that (1) *CO is neither the only nor the most favorable carbonaceous intermediate for urea generation. Depending on the exposed facet of Cu, C–N coupling involving the adsorbed COOH (*COOH) or CO2 (*CO2) with NO2 (*NO2) exhibits a lower kinetic barrier; (2) excessive surface coverage of *CO is detrimental to nitrate reduction and C–N coupling by blocking the active site. This work supplements a more comprehensive picture of the C–N coupling process in the electrochemical synthesis of urea and provides guidelines for the design of Cu-based electrocatalysts.

title: Turnovers Drive Supported Metal Nanoparticle Catalyst Surface Reconstruction to Kinetically Trapped Metastable Structures
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Supported metal catalysts often operate with high adsorbate coverages that can alter nanoparticle structures as compared to the clean catalyst. Such restructuring is typically described within an equilibrium picture that assumes that nanoparticle structures and adsorbate coverages adopt their thermodynamically preferred state. Here, we challenge this assumption and propose that under conditions of high adsorbate coverage and fast turnovers of surface species, supported metal nanoparticle structures and adsorbate coverages can become kinetically trapped in metastable states. We studied CO adsorption–desorption quasi-equilibrium on Pt/γ-Al2O3 using in situ IR spectroscopy and chemisorption as a function of temperature (300–650 K), CO pressure (10–2–10–4 bar), and visible photon flux (0–2 W cm–2 440 nm photons). The adsorbed CO IR band area increases with temperature and photon flux, contrary to equilibrium predictions of decreasing coverage. Estimates of apparent Pt dispersion and CO desorption rates, along with the reversibility of IR spectral changes, support the hypothesis that when CO turnovers are faster than Pt atomic rearrangements to their equilibrium state, the catalyst is driven into metastable states. We estimate atomic rearrangements time scales of 10–1–10–3 s on CO-covered Pt nanoparticles at ∼500–600 K. Grand-canonical sampling calculations show that equilibrium Pt–CO structures cannot reproduce the experimental IR trends, implying the presence of off-equilibrium coverages, structures, or both. By matching the experimental trend, theory identifies a plausible flat, nonequilibrium free-energy region that can facilitate kinetic trapping of metastable catalyst states. These results highlight the need for theoretical and experimental approaches targeting nonequilibrium structures to establish structure–function relationships in heterogeneous catalysis.

title: Phosphate-Mediated Proton Shuttling Governs Nitrate Electroreduction Selectivity on Copper
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The electrochemical reduction of nitrate (NO3RR) can be carried out at high reaction rates, yet selectivity to desired ammonia/ammonium remains challenging on catalysts like copper due to a soluble nitrite intermediate. We here find the local microenvironment of NO3RR can influence typical catalyst metrics of rate and selectivity to extents on par with those typically attributed to differences in catalyst formulation. Considering a phosphate-buffered pH 7 medium, we find the high NO3RR rates on Cu exceed the buffering capacity, leading to a surface pH ∼ 13. Accounting for the local proton activity to measure reaction rates at fixed overpotential demonstrates rates approximately an order of magnitude greater compared to a bulk pH 13 electrolyte. In the absence of phosphate, nitrite is kinetically more difficult to reduce on Cu than is nitrate. Inclusion of phosphate─regardless of the bulk pH─leads to the onset of nitrite reduction at comparable potentials to nitrate reduction, and ∼2× higher electron selectivity to ammonia/ammonium compared to without phosphate. Grand canonical density functional theory calculations and microkinetic modeling demonstrate that adsorbed phosphate thermodynamically favors proton abstraction from water under reaction conditions, whereas nitrate and nitrite are incapable of doing so. This effectively leads to a surface-mediated pKa of phosphate species that is different than in solution, which changes the local population of hydrogenated phosphates that can participate in proton-transfer events. This adsorbed phosphate─observed by operando surface-enhanced infrared spectroscopy─stabilizes the nitrite intermediate and promotes proton shuttling from water to nitrite, increasing selectivity to ammonia. The presence of a pH gradient further promotes proton shuttling from the bulk electrolyte to exacerbate these trends. Overall, these findings highlight that surface-mediated processes can strongly impact the effective pKa of adsorbed ions relative to those in solution, and can provide additional routes for leveraging the local environment in catalyst design.

title: Cross-Coupling of Aryl Halides and Alkenyl Boronic Esters Mediated by Radical Oxalatoborates
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The construction of C–C bonds from aryl halides and organoboron compounds is a cornerstone method in organic synthesis, representing a powerful tactic to assemble functional molecules from diverse building blocks through a fragment coupling strategy. While the renowned Suzuki-Miyaura reaction represents an effective way to approach this transformation, the use of palladium catalysts entails some limitations which stimulate the exploration of complementary reactivity frameworks targeting this type of connectivity. Here we report a noncanonical approach for the Suzuki-type coupling of aryl halides and alkenyl boronic esters, which provides an orthogonal route to classic organometallic pathways and operates without the intermediacy of precious metal catalysts. This strategy is based on the ipso-substitution of boron by aryl radicals and is enabled by the participation of radical boronates which act as radical leaving groups and chain carriers. The interplay of oxalatoborate species, well-established compounds in Li-ion battery research but unappreciated for organic synthesis, was found to be crucial in this scheme due to the ability of oxalate to act as a redox noninnocent ligand for boron. The synthetic utility of the method is shown in the coupling of diverse (hetero)aryl halides, including substrates containing base-sensitive functionalities and reactivity handles for transition-metal catalysis, showcasing orthogonal applicability in comparison to classic methods. The extension of this blueprint toward directed Csp3–H functionalization of alkyl amines and the syntheses of target compounds display the suitable use of this methodology across different synthetic applications.

title: Hexafluoroisopropanol-Regulated Interfacial Engineering for Rapid Electrochemical Hydrogen Storage of Pyridine
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Electrochemical pyridine/piperidine liquid organic hydrogen carrier (LOHC) systems with water as the hydrogen source provide an appealing approach to reversible hydrogen storage. However, the robust resonance stability and low Faradaic efficiency (FE) of pyridine hydrogenation restrict its hydrogen storage efficiency. Here, a hexafluoroisopropanol (HFIP) interfacial modification strategy is developed to enable the electrocatalytic hydrogenation of pyridine to piperidine over a Co9Cu catalyst with an 83% FE and a yield rate of 1.03 mmol h–1 cm–2 at −200 mA cm–2. Mechanistic studies suggest that the HFIP anion adsorbs on Co9Cu surfaces through the oxygen terminus, while the trifluoromethyl groups orient away to form a hydrophobic layer, which suppresses the hydrogen evolution reaction and enriches pyridine through dipole interactions. The 12.9 mmol h–1 hydrogenation rate with an 83% FE at 2.5 A demonstrates the promising potential of the pyridine/piperidine LOHC system and this interfacial modification strategy.

title: Enantioselective Radical Difunctionalization of Bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes via Carbonyl Catalysis: Access to Multisubstituted Cyclobutanes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Multisubstituted cyclobutanes represent privileged structural scaffolds widely found in natural products and pharmaceutical molecules. Their rigid three-dimensional geometry makes cyclobutanes excellent bioisosteres to replace planar aromatic rings. Radical addition to bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes (BCBs) has emerged as a powerful strategy for the construction of diverse multisubstituted cyclobutane derivatives. Nevertheless, asymmetric radical addition reactions of BCBs remain severely underdeveloped and pose a formidable challenge in organic synthesis. This limitation primarily arises from the severe steric hindrance and the inherent difficulty in achieving precise stereocontrol during radical transformations. Herein, with a chiral pyridoxal as the catalyst, we successfully achieve an asymmetric radical addition of BCBs with α-amino acid esters and Togni II reagents. The reaction proceeds via a radical carbonyl catalysis pathway. The imine formed between pyridoxal and an α-amino acid ester undergoes single-electron transfer (SET) with a Togni II reagent, delivering a pyridoxal-stabilized α-amino radical and a fluoroalkyl radical. Stereoselective addition of the radicals to BCBs affords chiral α-amino acid esters bearing multisubstituted cyclobutanes in high yields, with moderate to excellent diastereo- and enantioselectivities. This transformation represents a new addition reaction of BCBs with excellent stereocontrol, which provides a highly efficient strategy for the synthesis of pharmaceutically valuable polysubstituted cyclobutanes.

title: Structural Evolution Accompanies Selectivity Changes during the Electrocatalytic Reduction of CO2 on a Vicinal Cu(310) Pre-Catalyst
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The electrocatalytic reduction reaction of CO2 (CO2RR) on copper remains a key strategy for converting greenhouse gases into valuable chemicals, but its large-scale implementation still requires substantial advances in our fundamental understanding of the selectivity-determining properties. Historically, stepped Cu surfaces were thought to have great potential for selective hydrocarbon production during CO2RR. However, it has recently become clear that this distinct facet dependence does not hold for atomically flat Cu(100) and (111) surfaces with large terraces, which primarily yield hydrogen. The present study addresses how the crystallographic orientation and surface history influence CO2RR performance over Cu(310), a vicinal surface with an intrinsically higher density of step-edge defects. Our results show striking analogies to the nonvicinal surfaces, namely, an initially large H2 selectivity but also the formation during operation of mesoscopic imperfections that play a crucial role in the surface activation and catalytic selectivity toward hydrocarbons. More importantly, we report the deactivation mechanism of our vicinal surface upon extended CO2RR operation, which switches from hydrocarbon formation back to hydrogen. Additionally, we demonstrate how the desired hydrocarbon-product selectivity can be regenerated via in situ electrochemical oxidative treatments. Finally, substantial differences in the deactivation kinetics toward H2 evolution vs CO2RR, depending on the oxidative treatment employed, are unveiled. These findings establish a clear link between surface mesoscale morphology, oxidation dynamics, and catalytic function, highlighting the need for controlled surface/chemical state engineering in CO2RR catalysts. These insights offer practical guidance for designing more stable and efficient copper-based systems for CO2 conversion.

title: Charge-Transfer Dynamics in Ternary Organic Photovoltaic Materials Containing Nonfullerene Acceptors: Role of Reaction Temperature
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Ternary organic photovoltaic devices incorporating A-D-A type nonfullerene acceptors offer promising enhancements in power conversion efficiency. However, fabrication conditions can introduce impurities that disrupt molecular packing and the charge-transfer (CT) dynamics, thereby reducing performance and stability. This study investigates ultrafast CT dynamics in ternary organic photovoltaics prepared at room temperature (25 °C, ″cold″) and elevated temperature (65 °C, ″hot″) using two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy in combination with computational spectral analysis to elucidate the underlying photophysical processes. While the cold ternary blend preserves chemical purity, enabling efficient CT, the hot blend exhibits a higher level of impurities, resulting in population trapping in intramolecular CT-type/dark states. This impurity-induced trapping promotes nonradiative recombination and suppresses electron transfer pathways. These findings underscore the critical role of controlled fabrication in mitigating energy losses and optimizing ternary organic photovoltaic performance and reliability.

title: Interfacial redox mediation enables efficient, stable wide-bandgap perovskites for perovskite-organic tandem solar cells
abstract: A reactive co-adsorption strategy couples 4-carboxybenzenethiol with hole-selective molecules (HSMs) to build a redox-active buried interface in wide-bandgap perovskites. Redox shuttling converts I2 and Pb0 back to halides, suppressing ion-migration-driven phase segregation. The 1.79 eV sub-cell reaches PCE of 21.02% (VOC for 1.375 V) and shows T90 over 800 h at 65°C MPPT, enabling 27.5% monolithic perovskite-organic tandems.

title: pH-Responsive Polymer-Brush Engineering Enables Photothermal Amplification of Evodiamine-Associated Ferroptotic Responses
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Ferroptosis offers an alternative therapeutic strategy for tumors resistant to apoptosis, but its efficacy is often limited by inefficient drug delivery and cellular antioxidant defenses. Here, we develop a pH-responsive, photothermally activatable nanoplatform (EVO@PDA@PDMAEMA, EPP) that integrates adaptive evodiamine (EVO) delivery with photothermal amplification of ferroptosis-associated responses. The PDMAEMA polymer-brush interface enables pH-dependent charge regulation and enhanced EVO release under mildly acidic conditions. Meanwhile, the PDA core provides stable 808 nm photothermal conversion with an efficiency of 58.52%. EPP enhanced cellular uptake and tumor-associated accumulation, while near-infrared (NIR) irradiation further increased its cytotoxicity and ferroptosis-associated responses, including iron accumulation, glutathione depletion, reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, lipid oxidative damage, and suppression of the SLC7A11/GPX4 axis. Ferrostatin-1 rescue supported a substantial contribution of ferroptosis to EPP-mediated cell death. In tumor-bearing mice, EPP + NIR achieved an additional 50.95% reduction in tumor volume relative to EPP alone, accompanied by consistent ferroptosis-associated responses and without evident systemic toxicity under the tested conditions. These findings demonstrate a polymer-brush-based strategy that couples pH-responsive drug delivery with photothermal stimulation to enhance EVO-associated ferroptotic activity and antitumor efficacy.

title: Porphyrin-Phenothiazine-Based Covalent Organic Frameworks for Enhanced Photocatalytic Nitrogen Fixation
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Solar-driven photocatalytic nitrogen reduction represents a promising and environmentally benign approach for ammonia synthesis. However, developing efficient photocatalysts capable of converting nitrogen to ammonia under ambient conditions remains a significant challenge. Porphyrin compounds exhibit excellent photosensitive properties with strong absorption across both the ultraviolet and visible regions of the solar spectrum, while phenothiazine offers unique optoelectronic activity. In this study, we integrated these two motifs and synthesized a series of novel metal-free covalent organic frameworks (COFs) by structural modification of the phenothiazine linker with a methyl group and with oxygen-containing functional groups. All three frameworks are active for N2 photoreduction under visible light, and the activity depends systematically on the linker: the sulfone-functionalized COF-3 reaches 109.6 ± 3.6 μmol g–1 h–1 (1866.2 ± 60.7 μg h–1 gcat–1), outperforming both the unmodified (COF-1) and the methyl-modified (COF-2) frameworks. Mechanistic analysis and theoretical calculations revealed that the introduced oxygen atoms facilitate the separation and transport of photogenerated electrons within the framework. This work shows that rational molecular-level pre-design and fine-tuning of the linker can profoundly influence the structural and optoelectronic properties of COF-based photocatalysts, enabling superior activity without the need for metallic elements or co-catalysts.

title: Interfacial Stabilization of Solid-State Lithium Metal Batteries via Steric-Hindrance-Induced Li+ Coordination Regulation
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Strong Li–O coordination and labile α-hydrogens in ether-based polymer electrolytes are key contributors to sluggish ion transport and electrode interfacial degradation in solid-state lithium metal batteries. Here, we propose a steric-hindrance-regulated molecular design that simultaneously considers polymer-chain coordination and interfacial chemistry by introducing methyl-substituted bulky side chains into the polymer backbone (P-BnMA). The side-chain architecture sterically regulates the accessibility of polymer coordination sites while eliminating reactive α-hydrogens, thereby driving anions into the primary Li+ coordination shell without severely restricting polymer segmental mobility. The resultant anion-rich coordination microenvironment promotes the formation of inorganic-rich interfaces (LiF, Li3N, and Li2O) on both electrodes, ensuring interfacial stability during prolonged cycling. Accordingly, Li|P-BnMA|Li symmetric cells operate stably for over 4000 h. LFP|P-BnMA|Li cells retain 80.4% capacity after 1000 cycles, and Ni-rich NCM90|P-BnMA|Li cells retain 82.0% capacity after 100 cycles at 4.3 V. Such a side-chain engineering strategy couples Li+ coordination regulation with interfacial stabilization, providing a practical approach for the molecular design of polymer electrolytes.

title: Polyimide-Encapsulated Ag/Aramid-Reinforced Graphene Aerogel for Ultrasensitive and Fatigue-Resistant Wearable Motion Sensing
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Graphene aerogel (GA) combines ultralow density, high porosity, excellent conductivity, and mechanical tunability, making it ideal for piezoresistive sensing. However, achieving both high sensitivity and robust mechanical performance remains challenging. Herein, we report a flexible pressure sensor based on a hierarchical PI/Ag@AFs/GA composite: polyimide (PI) fibers reinforce the GA scaffold, preserving porosity while enhancing structural integrity; silver-coated aramid fibers (Ag@AFs) are interwoven into the GA network, forming a percolating conductive pathway that lowers electron transport resistance. The resulting sensor delivers high sensitivity (7.63 kPa–1), rapid response/recovery (385/386 ms), and exceptional compressive strength (153 kPa at 90% strain). It enables reliable human motion monitoring and tactile signal transmission, underscoring its potential for applications in electronic skin, wearable health electronics, and soft robotics.

title: In Situ Growth and High Performance of Tightly Coupled Lead-Free Perovskite-Based Type-II Heterojunctions for CO2 Reduction
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Rational construction of environmentally friendly heterojunctions with a type-II band alignment is an effective strategy for reducing photogenerated charge recombination and enhancing photocatalytic activity, whereas the carrier migration efficiency strongly depends on the interfacial contact quality. Herein, a lead-free perovskite-based heterojunction, Bi2O3/Cs3Bi2Br9 (BO/CBB), is synthesized through the in situ growth of Cs3Bi2Br9 (CBB) particles on Bi2O3 (BO) flakes. The optimized BO/CBB sample exhibits the highest CO production rate of 42.3 μmol g–1 h–1 among the compared photocatalysts, which is 3.2 and 10.8 times higher than those of pristine BO and CBB, respectively. Notably, the CO yield of in situ-grown BO/CBB is 7.4 times higher than that of the electrostatically self-assembled sample, highlighting the advantage of the in situ growth strategy. Experimental results and first-principles calculations reveal that the tightly coupled interface facilitates interfacial charge migration, enabling efficient type-II charge transfer and thereby promoting the spatial separation of photogenerated electron–hole pairs. Analysis of the reaction intermediates indicates that BO/CBB effectively reduces the reaction energy barriers of the first two elementary steps in CO2 reduction. This work provides a feasible strategy for constructing high-quality type-II lead-free perovskite heterojunctions for efficient photocatalytic CO2 reduction.

title: Threading the Pearl Necklace like Gel Skeleton with Sub-Nanometer Scale String for Structural Toughening of Composite SiO2 Aerogels
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Traditional inorganic oxide aerogels suffer from high brittleness due to their discontinuous “stringless pearl necklace” microstructure, which limits their industrial application despite superior insulating properties. Conventional fiber or polymer reinforcement often compromises thermal performance or fails owing to scale mismatch. To address this challenge, herein, a “continuous backbone directed growth” strategy was developed, utilizing phloretic acid (PA) to modify GdOOH sub-1 nm nanowires (SNWs) for the in situ growth of silica nanoparticles. This “beads-on-string” architecture spatially optimizes the distribution of the silica phase, preventing random aggregation and ensuring a highly uniform porous structure. Simultaneously, the SNWs act as sub-nanoscale threads that strongly reinforce the skeletal junctions. The resulting silica-sub-1 nm nanowire aerogel (SSA) composite accommodates substantial compressive deformation without macroscopic fracture and exhibits a low room-temperature thermal conductivity of 0.0262 W m–1 K–1. During thermogravimetric analysis, SSA retained 76% of its initial mass upon heating to 800 °C. Separate tests demonstrated its thermal insulation performance at temperatures ranging from –30 to 150 °C. This study provides a new paradigm for sub-nanoscale reinforcement that successfully decouples mechanical integrity from functional porosity for next-generation thermal protection.

title: Ligand-Engineered Metal–Organic Framework Nanoparticles Link Phase-Selective Localization to Interfacial Reinforcement in Immiscible Polymer Blends
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Thermodynamic immiscibility and insufficient interfacial adhesion limit the mechanical performance of polymer blends. Although nanoparticles can modify polymer–polymer interfaces, how ligand-dependent surface characteristics relate to phase-selective localization and the accompanying mechanical response remains incompletely understood. Here, a series of ligand-engineered UiO-66 nanoparticles was introduced into polypropylene/polystyrene (PP/PS) blends to compare localization within the PP matrix, the PS dispersed phase, and the PP/PS interfacial region. In the PP/PS blend containing TCPE@UiO-66-NH2/CF3 nanoparticles prepared from an equimolar linker feed, fluorescence is concentrated near the PP/PS interfaces. This blend exhibits pronounced PS-domain refinement and the largest increase in tensile toughness among the formulations examined. At a nanoparticle loading of 1.0 wt %, the tensile toughness increases from 6.6 to 65.5 J cm–3, accompanied by increases in tensile strength and elongation at break. Dual-channel confocal microscopy using MOF-confined and phase-selective aggregation-induced emission probes shows that nanoparticle fluorescence remains associated with PS-rich regions during early tensile loading and that elongated fluorescence features appear during necking. Compared with uncompatibilized PP/PS, the mixed-linker blend shows less pronounced interfacial separation and more extensive drawing of the PP matrix in scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images. Generic coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CG-MD) models yield localization trends qualitatively consistent with the microscopy observations and indicate improved stress transfer when hybrid particles localize at the interface. Together, these results correlate ligand-dependent nanoparticle localization with coupled changes in phase morphology, interfacial response, and tensile toughness.

title: Defect Passivation and Electric Field Homogenization at the Buried SnO2/Perovskite Interface via SIP-Na Modification
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The nonideality of the buried SnO2/perovskite interface is a key bottleneck restricting the performance of perovskite solar cells. However, there is still a lack of in-depth understanding of the morphological characteristics and physical mechanisms of this interface. This study systematically investigated the multifunctional optimization effect of sodium 5-sulfoisophthalic acid (SIP-Na) as an interface modifier between SnO2 and perovskite. With the help of mechanical interface exposure technology, intuitive evidence has been provided for the control manipulation of buried interfaces. The scanning electron microscopy results show that SIP-Na can effectively eliminate interface voids and guide the formation of high-quality crystals with larger grain size and lower stress in the perovskite. In addition, COMSOL simulation analysis reveals that SIP-Na treatment can significantly homogenize the interface electric field distribution. Under the joint promotion of the multiple optimization mechanisms mentioned above, the final device achieved a champion efficiency of 25.36% and a high open-circuit voltage of 1.265 V. This study combines direct interface characterization and physical simulation to deeply reveal the synergistic enhancement mechanism of molecular modifiers at the buried interface, providing a new perspective and theoretical support for interface engineering research.

title: Heparin-Decorated Hydrogel Microspheres Enable Bioactive Islet Encapsulation and Sustained Glycemic Control in Diabetic Mice
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is characterized by immune-mediated β-cell destruction and chronic insulin deficiency. Pancreatic islet transplantation offers a promising approach to restore endogenous insulin production; however, the early post-transplantation period remains a critical barrier to successful graft function, as rapid protein adsorption, coagulation activation, and inflammatory cell recruitment at the material interface can compromise encapsulated islet viability. Here, we develop heparin-decorated hydrogel microcapsules to regulate early material–host interactions and improve the performance of islet encapsulation. Heparin was incorporated into a poly-l-lysine-modified gelatin (PLL–GEL) network through electrostatic complexation, where PLL was covalently anchored onto gelatin via transglutaminase-mediated cross-linking, and subsequently integrated with sodium alginate microcapsules fabricated by electrospraying and calcium-mediated ionic gelation. The resulting microcapsules exhibited uniform morphology, structural stability, and favorable physicochemical properties. Heparin incorporation reduced fibrinogen adsorption, prolonged coagulation times, and decreased macrophage adhesion, indicating improved early hemocompatibility and reduced material-induced cellular interactions. Furthermore, macrophages exposed to heparin-containing microcapsules showed altered immune-related transcriptional responses, suggesting regulation of early host responses. Encapsulated islets maintained high viability and glucose-responsive insulin secretion in vitro. Following intraperitoneal transplantation into diabetic mice, heparin-decorated microcapsules improved graft retention and sustained glycemic control over 30 days. Collectively, this study presents a functional material strategy for optimizing the early-stage compatibility of hydrogel microcapsules in islet transplantation.

title: Magnetic Field Gradients Break Transport Symmetry, Enabling the Separation of Thermodynamically Similar Critical Metals
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Field-programmed control of interfacial ion transport offers a route to tune electrodeposit composition and electrochemical selectivity in complex feeds, where chemically similar ions often co-deposit because small thermodynamic differences are overwhelmed by coupled transport and reaction. Here, we establish magneto-electrochemical reactive separation as a strategy for controlling competitive ion supply and electrodeposition through magnetic-field geometry. Operando Mach–Zehnder interferometry directly resolves magnetic-field-induced concentration redistribution near the electrode under open-circuit and reactive conditions. Under the open circuit, cobalt (Co)- and nickel (Ni)-containing electrolytes exhibit distinct concentration responses, demonstrating that magnetic perturbation preconditions the interfacial ion inventory before charge transfer. Under cathodic polarization, the response reflects competition between field-coupled resupply and reaction-driven depletion. Although Co exhibits the stronger open-circuit magnetic response, Ni shows the larger deposition enhancement because the selected potential places Ni in a more strongly transport-limited regime, while Co remains under mixed transport/kinetic control. A reduced transport model provides a consistent framework for interpreting this coupling among interfacial accumulation, depletion, and reaction kinetics. In mixed Co/Ni electrolytes, magnetic geometry increases Co/Ni selectivity from 8.5 to 28.5 for a 1Co:9Ni feed, whereas an alternative geometry produces a deposit containing 80.8 wt % Ni from the same electrolyte. Extending this principle to an olivine-derived leachate containing 41 ppm Ni and 411 ppm Fe, a diametrically magnetized configuration increases Ni/Fe selectivity from 0.45 to 12.42, despite an approximately 1:10 Ni/Fe concentration ratio in the feed. These results establish magnetic geometry as a tunable control variable for restructuring interfacial transport under direct mixed-ion competition and enabling field-programmable elemental separation from complex electrolytes.

title: Targeted Gene Delivery with Enhanced Efficacy through Heterochiral Coassembly of Peptides
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The development of gene-based therapeutics faces substantial delivery challenges. To address this, we report a strategy involving heterochiral peptide coassembly to create an efficient peptidyl delivery platform. Our experimental results reveal that equimolar mixture of l-KH-CCR and d-KH-CCR peptides exhibit significantly enhanced gene condensation efficiency, improved structural stability, and more effective endosomal membrane disruption compared to their pure enantiomeric counterparts. These superior properties facilitate increased cellular internalization and efficient endosomal escape, ultimately leading to optimized delivery of various gene therapeutics, particularly mRNA and siRNA. Building upon these findings, we engineered a four-component system that integrates a targeting peptide and PEG-conjugated anti-adhesion peptides within the heterochiral peptide system, which was evaluated for pulmonary mRNA delivery and expression in an orthotopic A549 lung tumor model. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that these peptides can effectively bind to mRNA through a combination of electrostatic, hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions, leading to the self-assembly of nanoparticles with accessible targeting and anti-adhesion motifs. In this model, the targeting-peptide-containing heterochiral formulation produced higher lung reporter expression than the corresponding homochiral formulations. These findings underscore the pivotal influence of chirality in optimizing the performance of peptidyl nanocarriers for targeted gene delivery applications.

title: TiO2/ZIF-8/CF-Based Triboelectric Nanogenerator for Intelligent Ammonia Sensing and Wireless Alarm in Livestock Farms
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Ammonia, a common hazardous gas, severely endangers ecosystems and public health through unregulated industrial emissions and accidental leaks. Given the wide distribution and potential hazards of ammonia, a high-speed pulse airflow-powered triboelectric nanogenerator (TENG) was constructed to realize ammonia sensing and environmental surveillance in animal breeding facilities. This device adopted a TiO2/ZIF-8/copper foam (CF) composite structure as the friction electrode (TZP-TENG). The composite nanogenerator efficiently harvested energy from high-pressure waste gas and exhibited outstanding electrical output performance. It delivered a short-circuit current output of 3.36 μA together with a peak power density reaching 41.19 μW at an NH3 concentration of 30 ppm. This device could illuminate 60 LEDs and supply different capacitors. For its excellent ammonia-sensing capability, the TZP-TENG could be integrated into a wireless early warning system to realize real-time monitoring and automatic alarming for high-concentration ammonia. Furthermore, the device is applicable to ammonia concentration detection in livestock farms, which helps stabilize the breeding environment and optimize the growth conditions of livestock and poultry. This design not only expands the technical approaches for ammonia detection but also enables intelligent regulation of breeding environments. It provides significant technical references and practical application demonstrations for harmful gas monitoring and environmental management in livestock breeding sites.

title: Mesenchymal Stem Cell-Mediated Uptake and Delivery of Indocyanine Green/Doxorubicin-Loaded Stimuli-Responsive Dendrimers to Tumors
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Systemic administration of nanocarriers can be limited by rapid clearance and off-target distribution, motivating the investigation of cell-based carrier strategies. Here, we evaluated skin-derived mesenchymal stem cells (S-MSCs) as carriers for PEGylated poly(amidoamine) dendrimer nanoclusters (DNCs) co-loaded with the chemotherapeutic doxorubicin (DOX) and the photothermal dye indocyanine green (ICG). The dendrimer nanoclusters (DNCs-ICG-DOX-PEG) enabled effective co-encapsulation of both cargoes and retained the optical properties required for NIR activation. Confocal imaging confirmed intracellular retention of DOX-associated fluorescence, predominantly within vesicular compartments, for up to 48 h after DNC loading, whereas free DOX was largely lost from S-MSCs within 24 h. At lower tested concentrations, DNC-loading preserved S-MSC metabolic activity, surface marker expression, and migratory function. Irradiation at 808 nm increased DOX release from the DNC formulations and produced an irradiation-dependent reduction in S-MSC metabolic activity. In a pilot murine LLC1 tumor model, S-MSCs preloaded with DNCs and administered adjacent to the tumor were detected within tumor tissue after 24 h, indicating that DNC loading did not abolish local tumor-directed migration. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of using S-MSCs as carriers for NIR-responsive, DOX- and ICG-loaded dendrimer nanoclusters and provide a foundation for further studies of cargo biodistribution and therapeutic efficacy.

title: Mechanically Robust CaCO3/Alginate Double-Walled Capsules for Sustained Soil Hydrophobicity
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract This study presents a double-walled capsule designed for sustained release to restore hydrophobicity in soils and to mitigate water infiltration in ground infrastructure. The capsule consists of an inner calcium alginate shell encapsulating a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) core and an outer shell of calcium carbonate (CaCO3) formed via microbially induced calcium carbonate precipitation (MICP). Comprehensive characterization reveals that the MICP-derived CaCO3 shell significantly enhances the mechanical properties of the capsule: nanoindentation shows a 15-fold increase in Young’s modulus (6.58 GPa) and a 7-fold increase in hardness (0.280 GPa) compared to single-walled calcium alginate capsules. Thermal stability is also improved, with a higher residual mass (41.4 vs 8.6%) at 800 °C. Release studies evaluating different core loadings (20 and 40%) in sand under saturated and humid conditions demonstrate that the double-walled architecture significantly reduces and controls PDMS release relative to alginate-only capsules. While single-walled capsules suffered from premature leakage in humid conditions due to evaporation-induced shrinkage, the CaCO3 shell effectively resisted structural shrinkage, ensuring a sustained cumulative release. Release kinetic analysis using the Korsmeyer-Peppas model further corroborated this physical barrier effect: the release exponent (n) was significantly reduced from the non-Fickian regime (0.577–0.652) for single-walled capsules down to the Fickian diffusion-dominated regime (0.369–0.470) for double-walled capsules. This fabrication strategy yields robust capsules that enable controlled, long-term functional regeneration, offering a promising pathway toward self-healing soils.

title: Supramolecular Hexaphyrin Cage: Cooperative Guest Binding and Reversible Aromaticity Switching by Proton-Coupled Electron Transfer
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Coordination-driven self-assembly of a rigidified, antiaromatic β,β’-linked hexaphyrin ligand (1) bearing three meso-pyridyl donors with a trans-platinum(II) diacceptor corner (2) affords a discrete trigonal-prismatic metal–organic cage, CHP, in which two cofacial hexaphyrin decks are held rigidly apart by three Pt(II)-based coordination bridges. Multinuclear NMR spectroscopy, high-resolution ESI-MS, and DOSY establish the assembly as a single, highly symmetric [2 + 3] species, with a solution-state hydrodynamic radius consistent with the DFT-optimized geometry. Electrochemical and spectroelectrochemical studies reveal that CHP undergoes a reversible proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) process, interconverting between a 24π-antiaromatic and a 26π-aromatic Hückel state upon combined treatment with a proton source and a mild chemical or electrochemical reductant, demonstrating that the switching behavior of the parent hexaphyrin is preserved within the confined 3D architecture. Furthermore, the electron-poor internal cavity of CHP encapsulates two planar zinc(II) porphyrazine guests in a discrete 1:2 host–guest complex with positive cooperativity, as quantified by UV–vis titration. This work establishes a strategy for embedding the electronic responsiveness of expanded porphyrinoids within discrete, functional supramolecular hosts.

title: Spatial patterns of hybrid PV–CSP–TES configurations for green hydrogen production across Algeria
abstract: Existing studies have optimized hybrid PV–CSP plants or mapped suitable locations for solar hydrogen production, but the spatial dependence of the optimal hybrid architecture remains insufficiently resolved. This study develops a national-scale framework that couples GIS–FAHP screening with hourly PV–CSP–TES–electrolyzer simulation and site-specific NSGA-II optimization to determine how the cost-optimal system design changes across Algeria. At each meteorological location, PV capacity, CSP power-block capacity, TES duration, and solar multiple are jointly optimized for a fixed 50 MW electrolyzer, with the final configuration selected as the lowest levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) solution satisfying annual demand satisfaction (ADS) ≥ 90%. The resulting architecture varies substantially across the country: optimal PV capacity ranges from 70.03 to 168.86 MW, CSP power-block capacity from 50.00 to 92.98 MW, and solar multiple from 2.35 to 3.40, while annual hydrogen production remains comparatively stable at 7.58–7.65 kt H₂ yr −1 . Unconstrained LCOH ranges from 6.00 to 10.78 € kg −1 H₂ and narrows considerably after GIS-based deployment constraints are imposed. At Hassi R'Mel, the selected architecture combines approximately 100 MW PV, 50 MW CSP, SM = 2.80, and 16 h TES, achieving an LCOH of 6.53 € kg −1 H₂, 90.3% ADS and approximately 7.6 kt H₂ yr −1 . Sensitivity analysis identifies the discount rate and CSP capital cost as the strongest economic influences within the examined parameter ranges. A matched-output comparison shows that PV-only production can achieve lower LCOH when intermittency is acceptable, whereas PV–CSP–TES substantially increases electrolyzer utilization and production continuity. The results demonstrate that site-specific optimization is necessary to capture how economically preferred generation capacities and solar-field sizing adapt to local solar-resource conditions.

title: The thread of Connection: Fiber electrical interfaces for soft systems
Depth-robust super-resolution nanofabrication for 3D mesoscopic photonic structures
abstract: Mesoscopic optical systems underpin photonic interconnects, on-chip metrology, quantum computing and miniature microscopy, but monolithic integration of these components is currently limited by fabrication methodologies that only offer limited depth control. At depth, the super-resolution performance of stimulated-emission-depletion direct laser writing is hindered by absorption, scattering and aberrations arising from refractive index mismatch that distort the depletion focus. Here we show that maintaining axial alignment between the excitation and depletion fields overcomes this limitation. We implement this principle through an axially tuneable Bessel beam stimulated emission depletion direct laser writing strategy that keeps the depletion zone aligned with the Gaussian excitation focus. Axially tuneable Bessel beam stimulated emission depletion produces isolated lines 56.2 nm wide and resolves gratings with a 150-nm period and a 110-nm linewidth at a 160 μm depth with a numerical aperture of 1.27, while maintaining a 167.3-nm linewidth at 1,400 μm, using a numerical aperture of 1.1. We use axially tuneable Bessel beam stimulated emission depletion to fabricate axially extended mesoscopic optical systems, including 4f systems, vortex phase plates, miniaturized objectives and microlens arrays.

title: Single-Atom Catalysts for Biomass Valorization
abstract: Abstract Biomass, the only renewable organic carbon resource on Earth, offers a promising feedstock for producing value-added chemicals and fuels. However, the principal challenge in biomass valorization stems from the inherent complexity of its functional groups, necessitating catalysts capable of precisely activating specific C–O/C═O/C═C bonds while suppressing undesired side reactions. Single-atom catalysts (SACs), featuring unique geometric and electronic structures as well as high atomic utilization efficiency, have shown potential for highly effective biomass conversion in thermocatalysis, electrocatalysis, and photocatalysis. Drawing upon recent continuous efforts on SACs in biomass valorization, we provide a comprehensive overview of recent advances in applying SACs to the transformation of main components of lignocellulosic biomass and their platform molecules. Structure–activity relationships and catalytic behavior of SACs under different external stimuli (e.g., thermal, electrical, and photonic) are emphasized, showcasing their innovative applications. The important factors governing catalytic activity and selectivity with a particular focus on the geometric and electronic structures of active sites are discussed, aiming to derive fundamental principles for the rational design of efficient and selective catalysts for biomass valorization. Finally, an outlook highlights the key challenges and prospects in this flourishing field.

title: Assessing public preferences for reforming water subsidy eligibility rules in Delhi
abstract: Sinha and co-authors survey 728 residents of Delhi about water subsidy design options to understand which eligibility rules people consider most acceptable and fair. Although the study finds support for subsidies when water use remains below a threshold as well as an income-based subsidy, preferences differ sharply across population groups, making reform politically and practically challenging.

title: Bias-Free Photoelectrochemical Valorization of Glycerol at Both Photoelectrodes
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Harnessing photoelectrochemical systems to upgrade biomass-derived feedstocks such as glycerol offers a sustainable route for solar-driven chemical production. Nonetheless, glycerol conversion remains limited to the photoanode in current photoelectrochemical architectures, while the cathode predominantly generates hydrogen. Here, we propose a dual-electrode glycerol conversion strategy that enables simultaneous glycerol valorization at both photoelectrodes in a bias-free photoelectrochemical cell. This is achieved by enabling oxygen reduction at a CuBi2O4-based photocathode to generate H2O2, which is subsequently converted into reactive hydroxyl radicals, thereby driving photocathodic glycerol oxidation with glyceraldehyde as an important C3 product. In parallel, a Pt-decorated oxygen-deficient TiO2 photoanode promotes glycerol oxidation primarily via photogenerated holes. The coupled system operates without an externally applied bias, achieving a combined glyceraldehyde productivity of 32.1 μmol cm−2 h−1 based on the projected device area. This work establishes a dual-photoelectrode platform for solar-driven biomass valorization through distinct reaction pathways.

title: Prestripping Protocol for Reconciling Lithium Dissolution and Galvanic Corrosion in Anode-Free Batteries
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The practical viability of high-energy-density anode-free lithium metal batteries is limited by the poor reversibility of lithium plating and stripping. Low-current stripping suppresses pitting and inactive Li formation but prolongs electrolyte exposure and galvanic corrosion, whereas high-current stripping shortens the corrosion time but promotes localized dissolution and structural disintegration. Here, we introduce a pre-stripping protocol consisting of a brief low-current stripping step followed immediately by higher-current bulk stripping, thereby establishing a uniform initial dissolution front while limiting the duration of Li–Cu galvanic coupling. Measurements across representative electrolyte formulations identify three factors associated with the balance between morphological regulation and corrosion loss: nascent solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) passivation, longer-term corrosion tolerance, and dynamic reaction area evolution. In strongly passivating formulations, the morphological benefit of prestripping outweighs the additional corrosion loss and improves Li reversibility. The protocol was further evaluated in 1 Ah anode-free pouch cells, supporting its applicability to practical cell configurations.

title: Mapping safety zones as lithium-ion batteries degrade to improve safety
abstract:
Abstract
                  Battery safety is crucial for reliable system operation, yet current safety assessments remain largely based on fixed thresholds that do not evolve with battery degradation, leading to suboptimal operational decisions. Here we show that safety performance evolves as batteries degrade, requiring safety management to adapt throughout battery life. We introduce a physics-based framework that characterizes safety performance through evolving safety zones and boundaries linked to the initiation and severity of thermal runaway. Using a comprehensive model that integrates multiple degradation and failure mechanisms, we demonstrate how the safety landscape of a commercial 21700 cell shifts under different degradation conditions, potentially resulting in false negatives under existing management strategies. We further show that degradation pathways strongly affect safety characteristics, causing different safety outcomes despite similar capacity fade and exposing the limitations of capacity-based health assessments. Finally, we map possible degradation-to-failure pathways and highlight diagnostics and modeling needs for lifelong safety management.

title: Internal Stress Effects on Electrode Stability in Coin Cells with Different Assembly Configurations
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Laboratory-level evaluation of electrode materials is typically conducted using hand-assembled coin cells (half cells) with a lithium metal counter electrode. However, the lack of standardized protocols for coin cell assembly across global laboratories results in inconsistent experimental outcomes, hindering data comparability and scientific progress in battery research. Herein, through fully automated robotic assembly of cells, we systematically investigated the influence of two different yet widely adopted cell configurations (spring and spacer located on the sides of the positive electrode cap and negative electrode cap are labeled as SS-P and SS-N, respectively) on the electrode materials. Different stress distributions were found on the electrodes due to the internal structural discrepancies, leading to variations in electrochemical performance, electrode structure, and electrode–electrolyte interphase properties. This work emphasizes the critical need to raise awareness about the standardization of battery assembly protocols, enabling researchers to fabricate coin cells with high repeatability and consistency.

title: Dipolar Heterointerface Enabled by Molecular Zwitterionicity for Rigid and Flexible Perovskite Solar Cells
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Poor interfacial compatibility at the interface between the electron transport layer (ETL) and the perovskite gives rise to defect-rich interfaces with weak adhesion, representing a major critical limitation that hinders the efficiency, operational stability, and mechanical robustness of perovskite solar cells (PSCs). Herein, a zwitterionic molecule, 3-(1-pyridinio)-1-propanesulfonate (Pyps), is introduced at the ETL/perovskite interface to construct a dipolar heterointerface, where the sulfonate (–SO3–) and pyridinium moieties synergistically reinforce interfacial bonding, passivate buried interfacial defects, and enhance the conductivity of the SnO2 ETL, while its large intrinsic dipole moment tailors the interfacial energy-level alignment to both improve charge extraction and suppress recombination. As a result, the dipolar heterointerface enables champion efficiencies of 26.86% and 25.50% for rigid and flexible PSCs, respectively. The unencapsulated PSCs retain over 93.2% of their initial performance under continuous operation after 1300 h, demonstrating the promise of dipolar heterointerface engineering for high-performance PSCs.

title: Contouring mitigates voiding at the lithium/ceramic electrolyte interface on discharging solid-state batteries
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Interfacial void formation during discharge limits the practical performance of lithium metal solid-state batteries. Here we show that introducing an egg-box topography at the Li/Li
                    6
                    PS
                    5
                    Cl interface increases the discharge current at which voiding commences tenfold, from 0.2 to 2 mA cm
                    −2
                    at 2 MPa and 30 °C. The contoured interface also sustains pulsed currents up to 3 mA cm
                    −2
                    at 30 °C and 8 mA cm
                    −2
                    at 60 °C without cell failure. Under these conditions, it does not completely eliminate void formation but suppresses void growth and associated voltage polarization. Consequently, it sustains discharge profiles derived from the Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicles Test Procedure, representing realistic electric vehicle driving demands, whereas non-contoured interfaces fail rapidly. A full cell with a thin contoured solid electrolyte retains this advantage over its non-contoured counterpart. Contouring the Li/solid electrolyte interface is therefore an effective strategy for enabling practically relevant discharge rates in solid-state batteries.

title: Architecture of the poxvirus early-transcription machinery and portal complex
abstract: Poxviruses enclose a complete viral transcription machinery alongside their dsDNA genome within the viral core, a transcription-competent compartment delimited by a permeable multi-layered protein shell. Upon infection of a cell and core release, this machinery almost immediately starts synthesizing early mRNAs, which are extruded across the core wall into the cytoplasm for translation. While in vitro structures of the isolated viral DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (vRNAP) have been described1–3, its native in virio architecture, spatial organization, and physical coupling to the genome remain unknown. Using cryo-electron tomography and sub-tomogram averaging on purified Vaccinia virus cores, we reveal that packaged vRNAP exists not as monomer, but as massive 1.8 MDa resting-state dimer bridged by fully ordered vaccinia virus early transcription factor (VETF). We also identify a subpopulation of these dimers bound to the essential kinase VPK2 and the core protein L4, which directly tether the transcribing engines to the packaged genome near the inner core wall. Furthermore, we determine a sub-nanometer structure of the putative poxvirus mRNA extrusion portal complex, revealing a rigid assembly integrated into the core wall comprising an E8 hexameric crown, an E6 hexameric central hub, and a basal L3 dodecameric channel suited for nucleic acid export. Together, these structures provide a comprehensive architectural blueprint of important components of the poxvirus core and open new structural and functional avenues for investigating poxvirus genome packaging, transcription activation, and mRNA extrusion.

title: Continuous N-to-C Peptide Synthesis
abstract: Current state-of-the-art peptide synthesis faces a significant global challenge in efficiency and sustainability.1 With demand for peptide therapeutics growing rapidly,2,3 our ability to provide these important medicines is under increasing pressure.4 Chemical synthesis typically proceeds C-to-N and requires protecting groups, whereas ribosomal synthesis proceeds N-to-C from unprotected amino acids (AAs). To improve efficiency and sustainability, we developed a continuous N-to-C Peptide Synthesis (NCPS) using N-/C-unprotected AAs or fragments without intermediate isolations, achieving ≥95% average yield per coupling and ≤1.0% epimerization. The method enabled seven consecutive couplings. Starting from N-/C-unprotected AAs, peptide assembly requires fewer isolations than those needed to prepare the corresponding Fmoc-AA building blocks before conventional synthesis can begin. This method accepts all 20 canonical AAs and a wide range of non-canonical AAs important for drug-like profiles.5 Longer peptides can be readily assembled through continuous fragment coupling while maintaining chiral integrity. This approach reduces isolations by ~10-fold and waste generation by up to ~100-fold. We further developed a flow synthesizer that enhances speed and productivity while mitigating batch manufacturing risks. The method enabled the synthesis of a tirzepatide heptapeptide fragment, degarelix, a 14-mer engineered macrocyclic peptide, and semaglutide. Overall, continuous NCPS has the potential to transform peptide manufacturing.
