title: Unidirectional rolling of single-crystal graphene into nanoscrolls
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Transforming planar two-dimensional (2D) materials into rolled-up nanoscrolls has attracted broad interest, owing to the introduction of new degrees of freedom for materials design and property modulation. As one of the most representative 2D materials, graphene is a promising candidate for nanoscroll fabrication. However, the practical exploitation of graphene nanoscrolls has been hindered by the lack of reliable methods for precise control over structure and orientation, limiting their integration into large-scale electronics and optoelectronics. Here we show the aligned fabrication of graphene nanoscrolls via deterministic rolling of wafer-scale single-crystal graphene films during post-growth cooling, driven by anisotropic interfacial thermal stress from unidirectional Cu steps on vicinal Cu(111). The receiving nanoscrolls exhibit tunable thicknesses from 2 to 40 nm, and an approximately one-order-of-magnitude enhancement in photocurrent over planar monolayer graphene, together with improved conductance and carrier mobility. This process also enables the formation of adjacent wrinkle-free graphene single crystals, providing a promising strategy for wrinkle control in 2D materials.

title: Programmable synaptic and stochastic regimes in a monolayer hBN atomristor
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Electrically programmable control over distinct memristive operation regimes remains largely unexplored in atomically thin materials. Here we demonstrate a monolayer hBN atomristor in which electrical stimuli reversibly switch the device between synaptic and stochastic regimes within the same atomic-scale platform. Electrical, thermal, and low-frequency noise measurements across the HRS–LRS transition reveal regime-dependent signatures of localized Ag configuration in the monolayer hBN device. In the stochastic regime, stochastic fluctuations and switching probability are electrically programmable, whereas the synaptic regime exhibits stable potentiation and depression characteristics. System-level studies further show that the regime tunability can be exploited for both neuromorphic and probabilistic computing. These results establish electrically programmable dynamic regime control as an operational framework for atomically thin memristive systems, providing pathways towards reconfigurable energy-efficient computing hardware.

title: Promoted phase transition in perovskite heterojunctions via in-situ regulated 2D intermediates enables stable solar cells
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The formation of 2D/3D perovskite heterojunctions often relies on spacer-induced ion-exchange, which is difficult to achieve graded distribution of 2D species for efficient charge transport. Here, we report a phase-regulation strategy for formamidinium-based perovskites guided by pre-adding a full-composition 2D perovskite (hereinafter denoted as Pre-2D) into the FA-based 3D perovskite precursor. This approach enables coordinated control of precursor organization and interfacial phase evolution, resulting in bottom-up growth of phase-stable α‑FAPbI3 with vertically aligned 2D/3D heterostructures. The gradient architecture at the buried interface improves crystallographic orientation, suppresses defect-assisted recombination, and mitigates ion migration. The resulting inverted PSCs achieve a champion power conversion efficiency of 26.61% at room temperature with a high efficiency of 28.01% at 245 K, and 23.58% for mini-modules. Notably, devices retain over 95% of initial efficiency after 1100 hours of continuous MPP tracking and 1700 hours of damp-heat testing. These findings provide a scalable route to regulate phase competition and buried-interface energetics in FA-based perovskites, advancing the development of efficient and durable perovskite photovoltaics.

title: Catalyst-free thermal dehydropolycondensation for precise synthesis of silicon-incorporated polythiophenes
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Organic semiconductors such as polythiophenes (PThs) offer substantial potential for flexible optoelectronics. Incorporating silicon into the PTh backbone represents a promising strategy to enhance flexibility and tune electronic properties; however, conventional metal-catalyzed synthetic approaches lack precise control over polymer chain growth, yielding materials with poorly defined energy levels and relatively board dispersity. Here, we report a catalyst-free thermal dehydropolycondensation (TDP) strategy for the direct incorporation of silicon into PThs, producing a class of narrowly dispersed silicon-incorporated polymers. This thermally driven, radical-mediated mechanism circumvents the uncontrolled initiation and competitive pathways of conventional catalytic routes, enabling precise control over chain growth and yielding well-defined PThs with narrow dispersity (Đ = 1.2 – 1.4). The dehydrogenatively coupled diphenylsilane- terthiophene polymer (PS-1) shows favorable energy-level alignment and a hole mobility of 9.2 × 10−4 cm2 V−1 s−1. When employed as a hole-transport interlayer in inverted tin-lead (Sn-Pb) perovskite solar cells, PS-1 enables a champion power conversion efficiency of 23.3% with enhanced operational stability, surpassing the 20.8% efficiency of standard PEDOT:PSS-based devices. This work establishes a scalable synthetic route to advanced conjugated polymers, providing a versatile materials platform for optoelectronic applications.

title: A Phosphinidene‐Bridged P 6 Platform for Phosphorus Framework Editing, Fragment Transfer, and Derivatization
abstract: ABSTRACT White phosphorus (P 4 ) is an indispensable feedstock for organophosphorus synthesis, yet strategies for the controlled manipulation of P 4 ‐derived polyphosphorus frameworks remain rare. Here, we report a phosphinidene‐mediated strategy that converts P 4 into a phosphinidene‐bridged hexaphosphane, which functions as a versatile P 6 platform rather than merely an isolable P 4 ‐derived framework. This scaffold undergoes controlled P─P bond reorganization, P 4 release, phosphinidene transfer, heteroelement insertion, and selective derivatization, providing access to phosphorus species spanning P 1 to P 8 . Mechanistic studies with water, cyclic(alkyl)(amino) carbenes (CAACs), and N‐heterocyclic carbenes (NHCs) reveal dynamic phosphorus‐fragment transfer and carbene‐mediated framework reorganization through phosphinidene‐containing intermediates. Extension to aluminum(I) chemistry affords structurally diverse Al─P clusters that can be converted into value‐added phosphorus products including PH 3 and PMe 3 . These results establish phosphinidene‐functionalized polyphosphorus frameworks as promising synthetic platforms for the controlled molecular manipulation of elemental phosphorus.

title: Autosomal dosage compensation in aneuploidy and cancer involves transcriptional burst regulation
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Aneuploidy, resulting from whole-chromosome or segmental gains and losses, is generally detrimental to organismal fitness and is strongly associated with tumorigenesis. While sex chromosome aneuploidies are relatively well tolerated due to dedicated allelic dosage compensation mechanisms, the existence of comparable regulatory processes for autosomes remains debated. Here, we investigate transcriptional responses to autosomal aneuploidy and identify widespread dosage compensation across affected chromosomes. Using high-sensitivity allele-resolved single-cell RNA sequencing of monoclonal cell expansions spanning diverse ploidies and degrees of aneuploidy, we uncover consistent transcriptional compensation of both chromosomal gains and losses. This response operates in a region-specific manner across both complete and segmental aneuploidies, revealing an unexpected flexibility in dosage regulation. We show that chromosome losses are compensated through increased transcriptional burst frequency from the remaining allele. Complementary proteomics analyses demonstrate additional buffering at the protein level, resulting in a substantial, though still incomplete, restoration of stoichiometric balance across autosomal aneuploid chromosomes for both copy number gains and losses. Analyses of cancer transcriptomes confirm that compensatory mechanisms are active in human tumours. Together, our findings establish dosage compensation as a genome-wide and dynamic response to gene dose imbalance. This mechanism extends beyond sex chromosomes, supports transcriptional homeostasis, and represents a fundamental and evolutionarily conserved mode of gene regulation active across species and in aneuploid cancer cells.

title: Bacteria-induced TLR2 signaling unleashes multiple mechanisms to reduce Treg immunosuppression and enhance cancer immunity
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) support T cell priming in lymphatic tissues, but whether TLR stimulation within tumors also affects T cell function locally remains undefined. Here, we show that TLR2 signaling is necessary to promote CD8+ T cell-mediated tumor control by dual intravenous and intratumoral delivery of attenuated Listeria monocytogenes (IV + IT Lm). TLR2 signaling supports T cell priming in the spleen during IV infection, but unexpectedly, TLR2 is also critical for the activity of anti-Lm CD8+ T cells in tumors upon IT Lm injection. TLR2 signaling is unique among all TLRs in its capacity to drive a cDC2-dependent reduction in regulatory T cells (Treg) and destabilize Foxp3 expression. TLR2-mediated Treg destabilization correlates with increased tumor antigen cross-presentation and stronger antitumor CD8+ T cell responses. Ultimately, TLR2-dependent Treg depletion is required for tumor control by IV + IT Lm. These findings reveal a novel role for TLR2 activation by bacteria in tumors to reduce Treg immunosuppression and enhance tumor-specific T cell responses.

title: A macrocyclic peptide inhibitor of the antibiotic transporter NorA
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is a human bacterial pathogen with an array of molecular mechanisms to evade the action of antibiotics. Within the organism, efflux pumps provide a first-line defense mechanism, enabling broad multidrug resistance across antibiotic classes and the ability for the organism to evolve target-level resistance mechanisms. NorA is a key efflux transporter in S. aureus responsible for conferring resistance to fluoroquinolones, puromycin, and other cytotoxic compounds. Here, we describe an approach to develop peptide efflux pump inhibitors (EPIs) of NorA by leveraging chemical synthesis and design, structure-based insights, and screening approaches to probe NorA pocket engagement and S. aureus growth inhibition. Our cryo-EM structure reveals that a lead peptide NPI-5 inserts deeply into NorA’s substrate binding pocket by using two tryptophan-arginine motifs to bind an anionic patch within NorA, thereby stabilizing the outward-facing conformation of the transporter and halting antibiotic efflux. Further optimization of NPI-5 involving unnatural residues and macrocyclization yielded cNPI-7, a peptide which potentiates fluoroquinolones in vitro and in a murine bacteremia infection model. The successful development of potent and selective peptide-based EPIs provides an approach for inhibiting other efflux systems from pathogenic organisms.

title: Revealing the Atomic-Scale Degradation of Platinum-Based Intermetallic Nanocatalysts Upon Relevant Fuel Cell Conditions
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Platinum-based intermetallic nanomaterials are promising catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in proton-exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs). However, insights regarding their degradation under realistic PEMFC conditions still represent a knowledge gap. Herein, a systematic series of L12-Pt3M (M = V, Cr, or Zn) intermetallics with a similar structure, chemical composition, and morphology were synthesized, and their activity-stability trends were evaluated under conditions relevant to PEMFCs. Time- and potential-resolved catalyst dissolution were acquired and quantified through online ICP-MS using 1 M HClO4 at 65 °C, revealing that the first catalyst/electrolyte contact induces significant catalyst degradation before operation. During electrochemical operation, the anodic dissolution at 65 °C is substantially higher than at 25 °C, and a strong competition between cathodic dissolution and ion redeposition takes place. Identical-location electron microscopy analyses captured atomic degradation processes directly linked to catalyst electrochemical dissolution enhanced by temperature, providing new understanding for developing robust catalysts for PEMFCs.

title: Fast-Charging Sodium Solid-State Batteries Enabled by closo -Hydridoborate Anode Interlayers for Sulfide Electrolytes
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Sodium solid-state batteries may offer high-power operation through highly conductive sulfide solid electrolytes but remain limited by unstable electrode|electrolyte interfaces. Bilayer separators can decouple interfacial requirements if electrochemical compatibility, contact quality, and charge transfer are ensured. Here, the closo-hydridoborate Na4(B10H10)(B12H12) is identified as an effective interlayer material for sulfide electrolytes. Time-dependent impedance measurements reveal that Na3PS4 bilayer cells still suffer from severe instability, while Na3SbS4 and Na2.9P0.9W0.1S4 bilayers are stabilized by the hydridoborate interlayer. For the latter cells, the interface resistance is easily dominated by poor mechanical contact but can be eliminated under moderate stack pressure. Incorporating Na4(B10H10)(B12H12) enables stable cycling of Na2.9P0.9W0.1S4-based cells with a TiS2-based cathode and Na15Sn4/Na3Sn anode, delivering >90% capacity retention over 250 cycles and capacitor-like charging from 0–50% SOC in 30 s (82 mA cm–2) at 80 °C. The results identify closo-hydridoborate interlayers as key enablers for high-power sodium sulfide solid-state batteries.

title: Ligand-field reconstruction enables 4.7 V LiCoO 2 with suppressed chemomechanical degradation for high-energy batteries
abstract: Ligand-field reconstruction via bulk fluorine incorporation stabilizes the oxygen sublattice of LiCoO 2 , enabling outstanding cycling stability under a 4.7 V high cutoff voltage with suppressed surface reconstruction and chemomechanical degradation.

title: Chiral cobalt-catalysed electrochemical enantioselective C–P coupling via phosphinoyl radicals
abstract: Controlling the stereochemical fate of phosphinoyl radicals remains a longstanding challenge. Now a cobalt-mediated electrocatalytic strategy enables highly enantioselective C–P bond formation and access to diverse P(V)-stereogenic compounds.

title: An Electrically Gated Solid‐State Thermal Transistor for Energy‐Efficient Thermal Management
abstract: ABSTRACT Vapor‐compression heating and cooling systems dominate modern thermal management, yet their efficiency and scalability remain constrained by mechanical complexity and refrigerant‐based operation. Solid‐state approaches offer an attractive alternative, with recent demonstrations showing the potential for highly efficient, compact thermal control. Here we demonstrate an electrically gated solid‐state thermal transistor based on bulk single‐crystal barium titanate, achieving a switching ratio of 1.6, among the highest reported for bulk ferroelectrics. We further introduce switching efficiency as a figure of merit, reaching ∼8.52 cm 3 J −1 , more than two orders of magnitude higher than that of the highest‐performing reported thermal switch, PbZrO 3 . Unlike previous thermal switches that operate between two discrete states, this device provides continuously tunable thermal‐conductivity states, enabling transistor‐like modulation and amplification of heat flow. In situ x‐ray diffraction combined with first‐principles calculations shows that switching originates from anisotropic phonon transport between ferroelectric domains. Integrated into a proof‐of‐concept thermal‐management system, the device shifts the baseline temperature of a miniature human analog by ∼0.6°C at a cycle‐averaged power input of 33 µW cm −2 , approximately ninefold lower than a vapor‐compression heat pump performing the same task. These results establish ferroelectric thermal transistors as a programmable, energy‐efficient platform for solid‐state thermal management.

title: Green solvent-mediated extraction of biomolecules: opportunities, advances, and future directions
abstract: This work evaluates green solvents for biomolecule extraction, examining performance, mechanisms, sustainability and regulation. It highlights hybrid solvents and integrated biorefineries as opportunities for circular bioeconomy processes.

title: Correction to “Iron/NHC‐Catalyzed Regio‐ and Stereoselective 1,6‐Additions of Aliphatic Grignard Reagents to α,β,γ,δ‐Unsaturated Carbonyl Compounds: Asymmetric Variants with Chiral NHCs”
Stress‐Modulated Ionic Transport Limits Composite Cathode Kinetics in Solid‐State Batteries
abstract: ABSTRACT High‐energy all‐solid‐state batteries (ASSBs) require thick composite cathodes, yet these architectures exhibit heterogeneous reaction distributions that limit their performance. Here, we show that chemo‐mechanical transport switching governs the spatiotemporal lithiation behavior of such electrodes. By combining operando depth‐resolved diffraction with microstructure‐resolved and multi‐scale simulations, we link utilization gradients to the dominant transport pathway and demonstrate that the reversal of reaction fronts between charge and discharge arises from dynamically evolving transport limitations. This switching originates from the coupled reconfiguration of electronic and ionic transport networks during cycling. Particle breathing and interfacial delamination disrupt electronic percolation, whereas the contact‐mechanics model indicates that stress‐field interactions within the solid electrolyte (SE) can limit ionic transport. The model predicts that this suppression depends on the activation volume and elastic properties of the electrolyte and can exceed an order of magnitude as interparticle spacing decreases at high active‐material loadings. Our findings establish a direct link between chemo‐mechanical evolution and transport control in solid‐state cathodes, and highlight the need for SEs with low pressure sensitivity and sufficient mechanical compliance to enable high‐energy ASSB architectures.

title: Magnetic Switching of Exciton Lifetime in CrSBr
abstract: ABSTRACT Exciton dynamics in layered magnetic semiconductors provide a sensitive probe of the interplay between spin order and light–matter interaction. Here, we study thin CrSBr layers using time‐resolved photoluminescence spectroscopy in an external magnetic field, revealing a step‐like reduction in the exciton lifetime from 11 to 7 ps during the magnetization flip from the antiferromagnetic to the ferromagnetic phase. The reduction of the exciton lifetime in the ferromagnetic phase persists below the Néel temperature, as evidenced by its strong magnetic‐field dependence that disappears in the paramagnetic phase. Ab initio calculations reveal a one‐dimensional nature of free excitons, accompanied by a pronounced change in the oscillator strength across the magnetic phase transition, predicting a shorter radiative lifetime of free excitons in the antiferromagnetic phase of CrSBr, contradicting the experimental observations. This discrepancy is explained by strong localization of excitons at low temperature. We show both experimentally and theoretically that the observed magnetic switching of the exciton lifetime is attributed to a larger exciton localization volume leading to a larger oscillator strength in the ferromagnetic phase. The results show that disorder‐induced localization effects play a key role in exciton dynamics in CrSBr.

title: Partial Solvation Promotes Chlorate Formation on Sea Salt Crystal Surfaces
abstract: ABSTRACT Partial solvation creates interfacial environments that are neither dry solids nor bulk solutions, yet how this intermediate state controls chemical reactivity remains poorly understood. Here, we show that partial solvation at relative humidities far below deliquescence activates unexpected redox chemistry at ionic salt surfaces. Using surface‐sensitive X‐ray spectroscopy, we observe chlorate formation on Arctic sea‐salt crystals and an independent natural salt system following exposure to water vapor, whereas chlorate is absent under dry conditions. Chlorate formation is associated with partially solvated, MgCl 2 ‐enriched surface domains. First‐principles molecular dynamics simulations reveal strong interfacial electric fields and undercoordinated hydroxide environments, providing physicochemical conditions compatible with charge separation and radical‐mediated oxidation. Our results identify partial solvation as a previously overlooked regime for activating chemical transformations at ionic surfaces and establish partially solvated salt surfaces as distinct reactive environments bridging solid‐state and aqueous‐phase chemistry.

title: Rethinking Klebsiella pneumoniae vaccines: from protective immunity to rational vaccine design
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae infections cause hundreds of thousands of deaths annually, yet a licensed vaccine remains elusive. Current strategies targeting capsular polysaccharides and lipopolysaccharides show promise but face limitations due to the complexity of Klebsiella pathogenesis and incomplete understanding of protective immunity. This Review highlights the critical barriers hindering broad protection against K. pneumoniae. We argue that next-generation vaccines require a paradigm shift, integrating antigen discovery, systems immunology and translational models to define conserved protective targets and immune correlates. This holistic strategy is essential to predict vaccine efficacy and finally combat this escalating global health threat.

title: Bidirectional control of a metabolic transition by the GID ubiquitin ligase
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The GID/CTLH ubiquitin ligase is a multisubunit E3 conserved across eukaryotes. GID/CTLH has been implicated in a variety of processes, including metabolic regulation, cell proliferation, embryonic development and cell differentiation. However, our understanding of substrate recognition by GID/CTLH remains incomplete. Here, we characterize the regulation, specificity and functions of the putative substrate receptor Gid11 in budding yeast. We find that upon its expression during the switch of carbon source from glucose to ethanol, Gid11 associates with the core GID complex, likely assembling into a ring-like complex. Through systematic mutagenesis, we identify a negatively charged pocket on Gid11 that binds substrates carrying N-terminal degrons starting with threonine and define the Thr/N-degron motif. Such Thr/N-degrons are exposed upon co-translational removal of the initiator methionine, while escaping N-terminal acetylation. Finally, we show that during the glucose-to-ethanol transition, GIDGid11 targets for degradation factors linked to ribosomal biogenesis, amino acid, nucleotide and central carbon metabolism, opposing the established role of GID during the reverse transition from ethanol to glucose. Taken together, our results establish Gid11 as a bona fide GID substrate receptor and highlight GID as a regulator of metabolic transitions.

title: Single-molecule landscape of DNA replication pausing
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: A pause in DNA synthesis that occurs when the replisome encounters an obstacle could lead to genome instability. Although important, systematic identification of replication pause sites is challenging due to their low frequency and delocalised nature. Here we present a single-molecule identification of sites of replisome perturbation across a eukaryotic genome using long-read nanopore sequencing. For each single-molecule replication pause we determine the direction of replication, leading/lagging-strand identity, location and approximate duration, and whether the replisome resumed synthesis. Although pauses are largely diffuse over the genome, they are significantly enriched over transcribed features and correlate with transcription and R-loop levels. Transcription-replication conflicts are more numerous when head-on than co-directional. Finally, we identify genomic loci with a strong bias towards leading over lagging strand pauses, consistent with uncoupling of the helicase from polymerase epsilon. As one such locus overlaps with an epigenetically-regulated gene, we suggest that helicase-polymerase uncoupling resulting from replication pausing could trigger epigenetic switching.

title: Host control of rhizobial proliferation in soybean nodules
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The root nodules of leguminous plants contain rhizobia that proliferate and differentiate into bacteroids inside symbiosomes for nitrogen fixation. Hosts must tightly regulate rhizobial proliferation to optimize symbiotic benefits and avoid pathogenicity, yet the mechanisms governing this balancing act remain unknown for most legumes. Here, using in vitro assays and pectin-deficient mutants, we show that intracellular demethylesterified pectin (DMEP) directly constrains rhizobial growth in soybean nodules. Furthermore, we show that host factors HOF1 and HOF2 act as regulators of DMEP stability, binding DMEP to prevent its degradation via polygalacturonase. Genetically altered plants with modestly reduced rhizobial abundance exhibited significantly higher nitrogenase activity per gram of nodules, revealing the importance of host-mediated restriction of bacterial numbers in determining symbiotic efficiency. Our findings uncover an unanticipated role for cell wall components in controlling endosymbiont population size and provide insights into host–symbiont interactions, with potential implications for legume improvement and crop yields.

title: Highly Adaptable Electrochemical Lithium Extraction From Brine via Heterojunction Engineering
abstract: ABSTRACT Electrochemical lithium extraction from salt‐lake brines has received extensive attention due to its low energy consumption, environmental friendliness, and high efficiency. However, conventional electrode materials suffer from sluggish desolvation kinetics and competing cations intercalation (Na + ) in the diverse brine environment across the world. Herein, a heterojunction engineering strategy was proposed to solve the above challenges. A lithium titanium oxides (LTO) heterojunction was rationally designed and constructed on the surface of LiFePO 4 (named LFP‐SEF), which could expedite the desolvation process of Li + via the induced built‐in electric field and suppress competing cation intercalation via size sieving. Consequently, the LFP‐SEF‐based device consistently delivers outstanding lithium extraction performance in a series of brines (Na/Li ≈ 1–150) around the world. Even in the brine from southern Tibet (Dangxiongcuo Salt Lake) with a high Na/Li mass ratio of 150, LFP‐SEF also exhibits 83.72% capacity retention after 50 cycles with high separation factor (Na/Li ≈ 989.80; Mg/Li ≈1856.50). The exceptional performance is preserved as the device size increases from lab‐scale to production‐scale (1.5 m 2 ), demonstrating its excellent industrialization prospects. The concept of heterojunction engineering proposed in this work opens a promising route to industrial‐scale lithium extraction in complex brine environment.

title: Distinct mechanisms of CNV formation at the human 15q13.3 locus
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Human chromosome 15q13.3 is a hotspot for recurrent pathogenic copy number variants (CNVs) associated with schizophrenia, developmental delay and epilepsy. We generated long-read genome assemblies for 10 patient-parent trios and compared them to 581 population control haplotypes from diverse ancestry where this complex region is fully resolved. We find that both the long (“BP4-BP5”) and short (“CHRNA7”) forms of 15q13.3 CNVs arise predominantly by non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR) whose susceptibility has been promoted by large inversion polymorphisms. While three BP4-BP5 breakpoints cluster in a 2 kbp PRDM9-enriched recombination hotspot, most CNVs are structurally distinct and affect the disease-relevant genes ARHGAP11B and CHRFAM7A differentially. Population analyses reveal at least 18 distinct structural haplotypes in 15q13.3 and show that the risk for BP4-BP5 CNVs is stratified more than 10-fold depending on ancestry, with 68.4% of Europeans but only 5.1% of East Asians predisposed, establishing inversion polymorphisms as major determinants of population-specific recurrent CNV susceptibility. Comparison to six ape species indicates that the duplication architecture promoting instability expanded recently and is largely human-specific.

title: CD33-CD45 interaction in Alzheimer’s disease susceptibility
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: CD33 is associated with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) susceptibility. The AD-associated rs3865444C risk variant reduces splicing of the sialic acid-binding domain, increasing the sialic acid-binding isoform seven-fold. Here we identify CD45, a GWAS-associated AD risk gene, as an immune cell-specific sialic acid-dependent cis CD33 binding partner, whose phosphatase activity CD33 inhibits. CD33 loss improved microglial amyloid beta clearance and protected against amyloid beta-induced dendritic spine loss in microglial-neuronal co-cultures, whereas CD45 loss impaired clearance, aligning with detrimental effects of CD33-mediated CD45 inhibition. CD33-CD45 interaction frequency was increased in monocytes from rs3865444CC individuals versus rs3865444AA, as well as in AD versus controls, independent of genotype. An interaction between CD33 and PTPRC (CD45) expression in human brain tissue was associated with a pathological AD diagnosis and global burden of AD pathology, consistent with the cellular findings above. Together, our results link CD33-mediated suppression of CD45 with AD genetic susceptibility and systemic myeloid dysfunction.

title: A meta-analysis of genome-wide DNA methylation in endometriosis
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory disease affecting 10% of women, characterized by the growth of endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus. Through a genome-wide DNA methylation meta-analysis of nine independent cohorts (n = 1138 samples), we show an epigenetic dichotomy: the eutopic endometrium of endometriosis cases shows no significant divergence from healthy controls, whereas ectopic lesions exhibit massive, consistent hyper/hypomethylation. We identify 1824 differentially methylated regions targeting the HOX clusters, ESR1, and GATA2, key regulators of cell differentiation and hormonal response. This suggests that endometriotic cells possess an epigenetic identity distinct from normal endometrial cells. While most alterations reflect biological mechanisms shared across anatomical sites, distinct signatures exist between lesion types. By harmonizing independent datasets, our study provides a high-resolution molecular map of lesions and strengthens the evidence that DNA methylation drives endometriosis biology.

title: Dissecting the root-fungal interface in 3D reveals spatially distinct signalling landscapes
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Plant-fungal interactions in the rhizosphere influence plant health. Current understanding of these processes largely derives from in vitro flat plates, hydroponics and gnotobiotic platforms. However, fungal-plant interactions largely occur in soil – a disordered and granular 3D environment with heterogeneous elasto-viscoplastic properties – whose inherent opacity precludes direct visualisation of the infection. How the physical structure of such natural habitats influences interkingdom interactions remains unknown. Here, we introduce an optically transparent 3D jammed granular microgel matrix that mimics the mechanical properties of natural microenvironments. This platform supports long-term co-culture of plants and fungi, while being compatible with classical physiological assays. We accomplish a direct cellular-level visualisation of the plant-fungal interface. Specifically, host-derived signals prior to the physical contact trigger hyphal reorientation towards the root tips. Using spatiotemporally resolved transcriptomics we discover distinct pathogen-host ex- and in-planta signalling modules, which are associated with granular heterogeneous environments. Together, our findings establish an experimental platform for dissecting fungal development and pathogenesis with unprecedented microscopic and molecular resolution.

title: Data‐Driven Conformational Mismatch Design Enables Extreme‐Temperature Energy Storage in Copolyimides
abstract: ABSTRACT High‐temperature capacitive energy storage requires polymer dielectrics to combine a wide optical bandgap ( E g ) with a high glass‐transition temperature ( T g ), properties that are often difficult to optimize simultaneously through conventional backbone design. Here, we introduce conformational mismatch into semi‐alicyclic polyimide copolymers and identify promising monomer combinations through a multistage workflow integrating machine‐learning prediction of T g , density‐functional‐theory calculations of electronic structure, and molecular‐dynamics analysis of chain conformations. Incorporating a methyl‐substituted diamine yields Co‐PI‐tC, in which local conformational mismatch modifies molecular fluctuations and chain packing while suppressing thermally activated charge transport. Conformational entropy estimates derived from atomic fluctuations quantitatively capture these changes and complement conventional structural and electronic descriptors. The resulting Co‐PI‐tC film combines a T g of 271.52°C with E g of 4.28 eV, delivers a discharged energy density of 8.6 J cm −3 at 200°C with 90% efficiency and retains 6.7 J cm −3 at 250°C, setting a high‐temperature energy‐storage record among reported copolymer dielectrics. These results establish conformational mismatch as an effective molecular‐design strategy for reconciling thermal stability and electrical insulation in high‐temperature polymer dielectrics.

title: Author Correction: A sensitive red/far-red photoswitch for controllable gene therapy in mouse models of metabolic diseases
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds

title: Impact of ICRH-driven beta-induced Alfvén eigenmode on fast-ion redistribution and ion heating in EAST plasmas
abstract: In magnetically confined plasmas, energetic-particle (EP)-driven instabilities can induce redistribution and losses of energetic ions, thereby affecting plasma heating and confinement. In this work, fast-ion-driven beta-induced Alfvén eigenmode (BAE) excited by ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) was investigated in low-density EAST plasmas using experimentally reconstructed equilibria and profiles. Experimentally, strong ICRH led to a significant increase in ion temperature and plasma stored energy, accompanied by the excitation of an Alfvén eigenmode at 64 under 1.6 MW heating power, while no such mode was observed at reduced power. Continuum analysis identified this mode as a core-localized BAE. To interpret these observations, integrated simulations combining TORIC, ASCOT, and GTC were performed. A modified fast-ion distribution function was implemented to capture the strong velocity-space anisotropy of ICRH-generated fast ions. Linear gyrokinetic simulations reproduced the observed BAE frequency and identified a threshold in fast-ion pressure for mode excitation. Orbit-following simulations with realistic wall geometry demonstrated that the BAE induces significant phase-space redistribution and enhances the loss of high-energy fast ions (energy ). Separately, the ASCOT power-deposition analysis shows that the strong BAE reduces the collisional power transferred from fast ions to thermal ions, thereby suppressing the fast-ion contribution to ion heating and limiting the increase in ion temperature. As the measured BAE activity decreases in Phase B, recovery of this ion-heating channel explains the subsequent rise in ion temperature. These results clarify the interplay between ICRH-generated fast ions, BAE activity, and ion heating, and provide insights into optimizing fast-ion confinement and heating efficiency in future burning plasma devices.

title: Linear and nonlinear benchmark of gyrokinetic simulation of energetic particle driven toroidal Alfvén eigenmodes in ITPA TAE benchmark case
abstract: A new gyrokinetic code, TEK, was benchmarked in simulating energetic particle (EP) driven toroidal Alfvén eigenmodes (TAEs) in the simple tokamak configuration chosen by the ITPA-EP group for code benchmarking purposes. Linear benchmark has been well established by other codes, whereas nonlinear benchmark for this case is lacking. This paper presents, besides the linear benchmark, nonlinear results for both single- and multiple- simulations ( is the toroidal mode number). The nonlinear results are in good agreement with an analytical theory on zonal field beat-driven by Alfvén eigenmodes, partially verifying the correctness of the nonlinear simulations. The saturation level and the resulting EP transport are examined. This provides data for future inter-code nonlinear benchmarking. In TEK, all species (electrons, thermal ions, EPs) are treated on the same footing using the gyrokinetic model (with electrons in the zero Larmor radius limit). The electromagnetic cancellation problem is mitigated by using the mixed-variable pullback method. Numerical details related to electromagnetic gyrokinetic simulation are discussed.

title: Sensitive, Flexible Circularly Polarized Light Detection Driven by Circular Bulk Photovoltaic Effect in Lead‐Free Double Perovskite Ferroelectrics
abstract: ABSTRACT Circular bulk photovoltaic effect (CBPV) of ferroelectric materials can be utilized as a distinctive methodology to detect circularly polarized light (CPL), especially in the system of organic–inorganic hybrid perovskite ferroelectrics. However, currently reported CBPV predominantly focuses on lead‐containing hybrid perovskite ferroelectrics and the resultant CPL detectors are generally based on bulk crystals, hindering further applications of those materials. Here, sensitive, flexible CPL detection is successfully realized by using lead‐free double perovskite ferroelectrics, (C 6 H 5 CH 2 NH 3 ) 2 CsAgBiBr 7 (BCAB). Along with the spontaneous polarization, BCAB presents intriguing CBPV, which drives photovoltaic current highly dependent on the helicity of CPL. Consequently, CPL detectors using BCAB crystals deliver robust anisotropy factor up to 0.68 and high detectivity of 8.5 × 10 12 Jones at zero bias. More notably, BCAB single‐crystalline thin films can be obtained by mechanical exfoliation from its bulk crystals, allowing for flexible self‐powered CPL detection with a high anisotropy factor of 0.63 at specific bending angle. The value of 0.63 reaches the highest value among the reported flexible perovskite CPL detectors. As a proof‐of‐concept, our work offers a novel path to realize sensitive, flexible CPL detection and would be helpful to design lead‐free hybrid perovskite ferroelectrics for other advanced chiroptical devices.

title: Vibrational Strong Coupling of Hydrogen‐Bonding Solvent Modes Modulates Proton Transfer in Wieland–Miescher Ketone Synthesis
abstract: ABSTRACT Vibrational strong coupling (VSC) is emerging as an efficient tool for influencing chemical reactions within an optical cavity. Here, we report the enhancement of ground‐state proton transfer in a multistep Robinson annulation reaction by directly coupling the cavity mode to a selective solvent vibrational mode that is absent in the reactants. Being a hydrogen‐bond‐donating solvent, methanol facilitates proton transfer via a hydrogen‐bonding network, and this proton transfer is further enhanced under VSC. An increase in the product formation upon coupling to the solvent O─H and reactant C═O stretch suggests a unique role of the cavity‐coupling of specific vibrational modes involved in the rate‐determining step (RDS) of the reaction. In this context, the intrinsic intramolecular vibrational energy redistribution (IVR) lifetime of the two modes acts as a key factor in determining the reaction outcome under VSC. Moreover, we find that VSC involving these modes also impacts stereoselectivity, leading to an increased enantiomeric excess (ee). This demonstration of enhanced yield and enantioselectivity under VSC highlights the pivotal role of solvent‐mode coupling in facilitating ground‐state proton transfer through hydrogen‐bonding networks, paving the way for mode‐selective control in complex multistep reactions.

title: Pregnancy rewires the brain — scientists are finally mapping it
abstract: Brain scans show what healthy pregnancy looks like, and offer clues about how depression and pre-eclampsia arise.

title: Mini microscope captures brain activity while mice are on the go
abstract: A head-mounted device records neuronal activity as mice explore a naturalistic environment and interact with each other. Specialists discuss the technology and its applications.

title: Tritium breeding lifetime assessment of a ceramic-based blanket in a fusion tokamak device
abstract: Achieving tritium self-sufficiency is a critical requirement for the viability of future fusion power plants. Here, a comprehensive assessment of the operational lifetimes of ceramic breeder materials under neutron irradiation within a tokamak environment is presented, focusing on the evolution of the tritium breeding ratio (TBR) over reactor-relevant timescales. This is defined here as the operational timeframe at which the TBR is maintained above a critical threshold of 1.10. Using the depletion capabilities within the OpenMC neutronics code, both conventional ceramic breeders (Li TiO , Li SiO , and advanced ceramic breeder—ACB) and emerging hybrid breeder-multiplier ceramics (Li PbO , Li Be O ) are assessed for operational lifetime strategies. Initial optimisation identifies breeder-to-multiplier volumetric ratios that maximise TBR at time zero, followed by time-dependent simulations to quantify TBR degradation due to lithium depletion during service. It is shown that while higher initial multiplier fractions enhance TBR, they also accelerate lithium depletion, reducing blanket lifetime. Conversely, hybrid ceramics with intrinsic neutron multiplication show reduced sensitivity to additional multipliers. A novel layer-wise optimisation approach, varying breeder and multiplier distributions radially and poloidally, is shown to extend blanket lifetimes and maintain TBR above the critical threshold for longer periods demonstrating lifetime limitations may be elsewhere within the breeder blanket. Verification against FISPACT-II confirms the accuracy of the OpenMC depletion methodology utilised. The results highlight the importance of spatially optimised material distributions and lithium inventory management in maximising breeder blanket longevity. This work provides a robust framework for the design of next-generation solid breeder blankets, offering practical strategies to minimise replacement frequency and support sustainable fusion energy.

title: Entropy Engineering Accelerates High-Temperature Oxygen Evolution Reaction Rate via Spin Manipulation
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The high-temperature oxygen evolution reaction (OER) activity is closely correlated to the spin state of transition metals in perovskite anodes. However, the roles of entropy engineering in modulating the spin state and influencing high-temperature OER kinetics remain poorly understood. Herein, we demonstrate that entropy engineering of La0.7Sr0.3FeO3−δ to (SmNdPrLaBaSrCa)FeO3−δ (SNPLBSCF) induces a transition of B-site Fe species from high-spin to low-spin states. This transition enhances the d–p hybridization of Fe–O bonds, lowers the energy barriers for electron transfer and oxygen ion migration, and finally accelerates the high-temperature OER kinetics. Consequently, the SNPLBSCF anode in a solid oxide electrolysis cell (SOEC) achieves a current density of 3.64 A·cm–2 at 800 °C and 1.6 V, outperforming most reported anodes. This work not only provides fundamental insights into the spin state-activity relationships of perovskite oxides but also offers a viable strategy for the rational design of highly efficient SOEC anodes through entropy engineering.

title: Resolving Chlorine Sites in Pharmaceuticals by Integrated Site-Resolved Zeeman-Perturbed NQR, Solid-State NMR, and Electron Diffraction Crystallography
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Many active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and high-value chemicals feature covalently bonded chlorine functionalities that influence molecular packing, stability, and bioavailability. However, site-resolved structural characterization of chlorine sites in powders remains challenging, especially in systems with multiple chemically or crystallographically nonequivalent sites, disorder, or hydration sensitivity. We report here a novel combined 35Cl nuclear quadrupole resonance (NQR), 35Cl Zeeman-perturbed NQR (Zp-NQR), 35Cl solid-state NMR, and three-dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED/microcrystal electron diffraction) approach to characterizing powdered chlorine-bearing chemicals. Case studies of ketoconazole and chloramine-T demonstrate the utility of the approach in characterizing local structural heterogeneity and the hydration state. The role of crystal packing and noncovalent interactions on the spectroscopic observables is provided through an analysis of chlorzoxazone and five of its cocrystals, of which three are novel. Compared to ultrahigh-field NMR spectra alone, NQR and Zp-NQR spectra provide improved sensitivity to small changes in the electric field gradient and in the degree of disorder around chlorine. Experimental NQR/Zp-NQR data combined with gauge-including projector augmented-wave density functional theory (GIPAW-DFT) provide local structural constraints for a partially dehydrated chloramine-T phase. The refinement protocol does not require single crystals, and in the case of NQR experiments, intact tablets containing APIs are analyzed directly without further treatment or grinding. As a proof of principle, commercial tablets are shown to contain ketoconazole in the same crystalline form as that seen for the pure API. The general approach could be extended to other complex solids incorporating quadrupolar nuclei and is not limited to solid-form screening, polymorph identification, and differentiation of salts and cocrystals.

title: Direct-to-Biology Bifunctional Screening Reveals Noncanonical Mechanisms of Targeted Protein Degradation
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Targeted protein degradation (TPD) has emerged as a powerful strategy for modulating protein function through small-molecule-induced proximity between a protein of interest (POI) and typically an E3 ubiquitin ligase to promote its proteasomal degradation. Despite significant progress, most degraders co-opt a narrow set of E3 ubiquitin ligases, motivating mechanistically agnostic strategies for discovering new routes to degradation. Here, we pursued a “degrader-first” approach using direct-to-biology (D2B) synthesis to construct and screen a 114-member library of BRD4-targeting bifunctional molecules to identify chemically tractable ligases that support TPD. Multiple compounds were found to induce Cullin-RING ligase (CRL)-dependent degradation, and two top hits were selected for mechanistic characterization. Unexpectedly, neither operates through canonical heterobifunctional E3 recruitment. Instead, one undergoes oxidative activation to generate a reactive electrophile that promotes degradation through DCAF11- or DCAF16-containing CRL4 complexes in a cell-context-dependent manner. The second acts through a bivalent bromodomain-binding mechanism that likely induces target conformational contraction and potentiates endogenous CRL3–SPOP-mediated ubiquitination. These findings highlight the capacity of D2B discovery approaches to expose noncanonical modalities of TPD while underscoring the importance of rigorous mechanistic deconvolution in interpreting screening-derived degraders.

title: Enantioconvergent N -Alkylation of Indoles with Alcohols Promoted by an Axially Chiral Iridacycle
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Achieving chemo- and enantioselective N-substitution of indoles presents significant challenges for catalytic method development. Herein, we report an enantioconvergent N-substitution of indoles with racemic secondary alcohols enabled by a newly developed axially chiral biaryl-supported iridacycle and chiral phosphoric acid. This borrowing-hydrogen process proceeds through an intriguing sequence involving transfer hydrogenation of indole, enantioselective reductive amination of an indoline intermediate, and subsequent rearomatization. Controlled reaction temperatures also enable selective access to the N-substituted indolines prior to rearomatization. The catalytic process accommodates diverse indoles and unactivated secondary alcohols without additional stoichiometric reagents, providing a direct and atom-economical approach to enantioenriched N-substituted indoles, including analogs of established drug candidates.

title: Halogenated Triazole-Based Metal–Organic Framework Achieves Ultra-Selective CO2 Capture under Humid Conditions
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Selective CO2 capture from humid, N2-rich flue gas requires adsorbents that combine extreme CO2/N2 discrimination with robustness under realistic conditions. However, only a few MOFs are able to combine ultrahigh selectivity, humidity tolerance, scalable synthesis, and structural durability. Here, we introduce CALF-20-X (X = Cl or Br) halogentriazolate–oxalate Zn-MOFs and a PVDF composite, integrating these attributes into an ultramicroporous framework. The halogenated Zn-MOFs are obtained by means of solvent-minimized liquid-assisted grinding followed by water-incubation route, producing a highly crystalline material. Halogen functionalization polarizes the triazolate C–H donor, thereby promoting directional C–H···O(CO2) contacts and enhancing electrostatic complementarity, as evidenced by an experimental isosteric heat of adsorption of 48 kJ/mol. Furthermore, this halogen substitution significantly restricts the size of the pore window inhibiting N2 uptake, and leads to the formation of perfectly CO2-fitted pockets. These combined features enabled a CO2 excellent adsorption of 2.89 mmol g–1 at 0.15 bar and 298 K, and CO2/N2 selectivity higher than 4074 for CALF-20-Cl, exceeding leading physisorbent benchmarks. The highly selective CO2 capture was confirmed by dynamic breakthrough experiments performed on a CALF-20-Cl@PVDF composite under humid conditions over numerous cycles, thus demonstrating its robust performance under flue-gas-relevant conditions. Competitive CO2/H2O breakthrough experiments, supported by GCMC simulations, demonstrate that CO2 sorption is favored at 21% relative humidity (RH), resulting in a 56% suppression of water uptake, and even remains competitive at RH > 50% and 318 K, a temperature relevant for carbon capture from point sources. These results highlight halogen-driven structural engineering for regenerable and humidity-tolerant next-generation CO2-selective MOF adsorbents with complete retention of the performance metrics.

title: Elusive *CH–*CHO Coupling Pathway for High-Performance CO2 Electroreduction to n-Propanol
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to high-value n-propanol represents a promising yet challenging route toward sustainable carbon utilization. However, its practical implementation is severely hindered by low selectivity and activity, primarily originating from the high energy barrier involved in the rate-limiting *C2–*C1 coupling step. Herein, we have successfully constructed an elusive *CH–*CHO coupling pathway on a stable Janus Cu2+/Cu0 catalyst, enabling low-barrier *C2 intermediate formation and highly selective n-propanol production. Leveraging the strong electron-accepting capacity of Cu2+ sites, key *CHO intermediates are strongly adsorbed and driven toward deep reduction to *CH species, effectively overcoming the critical five-electron transfer bottleneck for *CH generation. Meanwhile, adjacent Cu0 sites provide moderate and balanced adsorption of *CHO intermediates, allowing their asymmetric coupling with the Cu2+-stabilized *CH via a markedly low energy barrier, synergistically steering the reaction along the favorable *CH–*CHO pathway. In situ fiber-optic guided ATR-FTIR spectroscopy provides evidence for the coexistence of *CHO and *CHx-related intermediates, while DFT calculations further support the proposed *CH–*CHO coupling pathway. Accordingly, the Janus Cu2+/Cu0 catalyst achieves a high n-propanol Faradaic efficiency of 18.1% at a partial current density of 72.4 mA cm–2, alongside remarkable stability. This work establishes the *CH–*CHO pathway as a powerful strategy for kinetically favorable C–C coupling, opening a new mechanistic avenue for efficient conversion of CO2 to multicarbon via electrosynthesis.

title: Author Correction: Synthetic super-enhancers enable precision viral immunotherapy
An Allosteric CLR N-Terminal Swing-Out Mechanism for RAMP-Mediated Adrenomedullin Receptor Selectivity
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Three receptor activity-modifying proteins (RAMP1–3) form heterodimers with the calcitonin (CTR) and calcitonin-like (CLR) G protein-coupled receptors and determine their selectivity for six CGRP family peptide agonists. These ligand–receptor systems are drug targets for migraine headache, diabetes and obesity, and circulatory system disorders. Here, we used molecular dynamics simulations and pharmacological assays of receptor chimeras and point mutants to identify a crucial allosteric component of the mechanism by which RAMP2 and RAMP3 modulate CLR to confer selectivity for two adrenomedullin (AM) peptides. We found that the extracellular domain (ECD) of RAMP2 and RAMP3, but not RAMP1, stabilized a partially unwound “swing-out” conformation of the CLR ECD N-terminal α-helix to accommodate the unique binding mode of the midregion of the AM peptides. The inability of the CTR N-terminus to adopt the swing-out conformation contributed to the distinct peptide selectivity profile of the three CTR-RAMP amylin receptors. By exploiting the CLR swing-out conformation, we engineered AM antagonist peptide variants with enhanced affinity and selectivity for CLR-RAMP2 and -RAMP3. Our results reveal the long-sought mechanism of RAMP-altered CLR ligand selectivity and have significant implications for drug development targeting the CLR- and CTR-RAMP complexes.

title: Chemical Programming of Stacking Order and Superconductivity Dimensionality in NbSe 2–x Te x Polytypic Heterostructures
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Layered transition-metal dichalcogenides exhibit electronic states highly sensitive to lattice symmetry, yet elucidating the structure–superconductivity relationship has been challenging due to the lack of a continuous structural evolution within a single material system. Here, we establish NbSe2–xTex as a model system, where Te substitution drives a sequential polytypic transition across the full composition range─from the low-Te 2H phase, through mixed 1H/1T heterostructured 4H and 6R polytypes at intermediate substitution, to ideal 1T and distorted 1T′ structures at high Te content. Combining comprehensive characterizations, we map both the structural evolution and the accompanying changes in spectral weight and orbital character near the Fermi level. Electrical transport measurements reveal a striking phase-dependent superconducting dimensionality: the 4H phase (NbSe1.4Te0.6) exhibits enhanced anisotropy and an anomalous boost in the in-plane upper critical field, while the 6R phase (NbSe1.2Te0.8) shows suppressed Tc (∼2.8 K) and three-dimensional-like behavior. The combined electronic-structure and superconducting results connect the stacking sequence to effective interlayer coherence and the local spin–orbit environment. SOC band calculations resolve the distinct symmetry constraints on the 4H and 6R electronic states. These mechanisms fundamentally differ from conventional approaches by leveraging intrinsic, composition-driven polytypism to modify interlayer coupling and band structure. Thus, by establishing a definitive phase diagram that directly correlates polytypism with superconducting dimensionality, our work provides a clear roadmap for the rational design of low-dimensional superconducting devices through stacking-sequence engineering.

title: A Unique Conformationally Assisted [2+2] Configuration in Cycloparaphenylenes Enables Efficient Laser Devices
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Two π-conjugated macrocycles, namely the well-known [12]cycloparaphenylene and a newly designed macrocycle combining benzenes and rigid stilbene units, are presented for the first time as light-amplifying gain media in distributed feedback (DFB) laser devices. Both systems show good photonic functionality arising from a four-state photonic cycle comprising a [2+2] state configuration (two delocalized and two conformationally distorted localized states). The mechanism involves the generation of two optically coupled states through excited-state structural distortion induced during internal conversion, which reduces light reabsorption losses and promotes rapid population inversion. Comprehensive steady-state absorption and fluorescence and transient absorption spectroscopy studies are conducted in order to reveal the nature of the low energy lying excited states. Furthermore, amplified spontaneous emission studies of the compounds in polystyrene thin films, followed by the preparation and characterization of optically pumped DFB lasers, were performed. The results reveal new properties of these multifunctional cyclic π-conjugated molecules and unique structure-property relationships.

title: Experimental and Computational Identification of Wide-Gap Quaternary Oxychalcogenides BaZn2OS2 and SrZn2OSe2
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Oxychalcogenides have attracted attention as candidates for wide-gap p-type semiconductors in view of the energetically high and spatially spread characteristics of their valence electronic states. An appropriate choice of constituent cations would also enable n-type doping. However, reports on p-type doping have been mostly limited to Cu-based systems, which exhibit a strong p-type tendency due to hole generation and electron compensation by native Cu-vacancy acceptors. Oxychalcogenides with a practical level of n-type conductivity are yet to be developed. In this study, we focus on oxychalcogenides in the Ae–Zn–O–Ch (Ae = Ca, Sr, Ba; Ch = S, Se) quaternary system to explore new wide-gap semiconductors. Two as-yet-unreported compounds with wide band gaps, namely BaZn2OS2 and SrZn2OSe2, have been synthesized, along with four previously reported oxychalcogenides. First-principles calculations indicate that both BaZn2OS2 and SrZn2OSe2 feature direct-type band structures with low electron and hole effective masses, comparable to related compounds. Carrier compensation by native defects, however, is likely to make BaZn2OS2 insulating, whereas it can be well suppressed in SrZn2OSe2 by controlling the growth conditions. Systematic calculations of extrinsic dopants predict that bipolar doping of SrZn2OSe2 is feasible. Our results reveal the potential of non-Cu-based oxychalcogenides as a platform for the development of wide-gap, bipolar-dopable semiconductors, thereby stimulating exploration of related compounds.

title: Hypoxia-Driven, Self-Accelerating Immolative Photosensitizer Enabling Effective and Safe Photodynamic Therapy
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is an emerging cancer treatment modality, but its clinical translation is hindered by the persistent post-PDT phototoxicity of existing photosensitizers. To address this challenge, we herein report a hypoxia-driven, self-accelerating immolative photosensitizer in which PDT itself drives posttherapy detoxification. This is demonstrated with AIE photosensitizers with an N-oxidation-mediated photoinduced electron transfer (PET) feature, which creates a charge-separation state with pronounced electron–nuclear hyperfine coupling feature, enabling efficient intersystem crossing. This N-oxidation thus converts the highly emissive fluorophore TBP into the robust type I photosensitizer TBPO. Critically, the N-O bond could be selectively cleaved by cytochrome P450 reductases under hypoxia, immolating TBPO back to TBP. Unlike previously reported ROS-driven immolative photosensitizers, this hypoxia-mediated immolation does not consume therapeutic ROS and is accelerated by PDT-aggravated hypoxia. Consequently, TBPO exhibits a self-propelled detoxification mechanism, ensuring an initial high PDT efficacy while minimizing residual phototoxicity after therapy. Moreover, this transition process is self-reported by the fluorescence light-up. This molecular design achieves both potent hypoxia-resistant PDT and fail-safe posttreatment safety, addressing two long-standing barriers to clinical PDT. This paradigm shift offers a general design principle for therapy-fueled self-detoxifying photosensitizers toward outpatient PDT without lifestyle restrictions.

title: Nanoscale Flexibility Enables Low-Enthalpy Cooperative Water Sorption
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Passive, sorption-based atmospheric water harvesting technologies (AWHTs) have attracted recent interest as an alternative to energy-intensive condensation-based technologies. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) offer wide chemical tunability to design sorbents, but in practice, sorbents must retain moisture during humidity fluctuations, and small adsorption enthalpies are necessary for regeneration of the sorbent material. Here, we report that Cu(1,2,3-triazolate)2 nanoparticles with diameters less than 120 nm exhibit structural flexibility at the Cu2+ centers that enables a “breathing”-type cooperative water sorption. This cooperative structural phase change occurs only for nanoparticles that contain Cu2+, and not for the isomorphic magnesium triazolate. The phase change significantly decreases the onset pressures of adsorption and desorption compared to large particles and opens a practically useful hysteresis window in the isotherms, while maintaining small adsorption enthalpies (48 kJ/mol averaged over the isotherm, approaching the 44 kJ/mol latent heat of water at low RH). Mechanistic analysis indicates that adsorption initiates with weak electrostatic and dispersion interactions between water and triazolate rings brought into close proximity only by the distorted Cu2+ centers of the nanoparticles. Together, these results present a distinct water sorption mechanism and design strategy that leverages size- and metal-dependent lattice flexibility in a wide class of porous materials.

title: G:C:G:C-Flanked i-Motifs Are Thermodynamically Favored and Their Sequences Highly Enriched in the Human Genome
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract i-Motifs are biologically relevant noncanonical DNA structures whose stability is strongly influenced by capping interactions. Among these, minor groove tetrads (MGTs) are among the most powerful stabilizing elements identified to date, yet the molecular factors governing their effects and their potential biological significance remain poorly understood. Here, we present a systematic experimental and computational analysis of 16 MGT-stabilized i-motifs (MGTiMs), encompassing all combinations of terminal tetrad composition and orientation within a common sequence scaffold. NMR spectroscopy confirms that all sequences adopt closely related architectures, enabling direct comparison of the effects of tetrad identity and orientation on stability. Thermal denaturation experiments reveal that the stability hierarchy, previously observed in selected structures (G:C:G:C ≳ G:C:G:T ≫ G:T:G:T), is broadly maintained across the series, although substantial positional effects are observed. Molecular dynamics simulations and energy decomposition analyses suggest that differences in electrostatic interactions and local conformational flexibility contribute to these trends. Notably, genome-wide analysis of the human genome reveals a strong enrichment of sequences capable of forming the most stabilizing tetrads, with motifs containing two G:C:G:C tetrads reaching a 45-fold enrichment relative to random expectation. Interestingly, this most abundant genomic motif is also the only one that undergoes pronounced pH-driven conformational transitions, highlighting the unique structural plasticity of these architectures. Together, these findings reveal how tetrad composition and positional context govern MGTiM stability and identify NN-type motifs as a particularly enriched class of structurally distinctive genomic sequences.

title: Catalytic Enantiodivergent Neophyl Rearrangement
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The neophyl rearrangement is a long-established radical 1,2-aryl migration, yet catalytic enantioselective control of this process has remained elusive. Here we report a cooperative photoredox and chiral Brønsted acid catalytic system for the enantioselective neophyl rearrangement of tertiary alcohol-derived olefins. The reaction affords 1,5-dicarbonyl compounds bearing azaarene-substituted all-carbon quaternary stereocenters with up to 97% ee. Changing the radical precursor alters the preferred mode of catalyst recognition and reverses the absolute stereochemical outcome with the same catalyst configuration, providing access to opposite product enantiomers. The reaction also accommodates racemic olefin substrates, and experiments with the individual substrate enantiomers show that the chiral catalyst can counter their intrinsic stereochemical preferences. The results reveal how changes in catalyst–substrate recognition can alter stereochemical control during a transient radical rearrangement.

title: Radical Ring-Opening Polymerization of endo -Cyclic Monomers for Regioregularity Control in Vinyl Polymers
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Radical polymerization of vinyl monomers is inherently governed by propagation pathways that favor head-to-tail connectivity, limiting access to alternative backbone regioregularities. To address this challenge, we report the radical ring-opening polymerization (rROP) of endo-cyclic monomers, a class of monomers that has been largely unexplored in radical processes. Whereas many established rROP systems have been designed to introduce functional or cleavable units into polymer backbones, the present endo-cyclic monomers undergo selective rROP to generate carbon–carbon-backboned vinyl polymers enriched with nonhead-to-tail linkages. Copolymerization with conventional vinyl monomers was also achieved, providing access to copolymers with tunable backbone microstructures. In particular, using vinyl ketones and their corresponding endo-cyclic cyclodimers as structurally matched pairs, we accessed poly(vinyl ketone)s with systematically varied head-to-tail linkage contents. This control over backbone regioregularity translated into tunable macroscopic properties, including glass transition temperature and photodegradation kinetics, establishing regioregularity as a structural handle for controlling material properties. The strategy was also compatible with controlled radical polymerization, enabling the synthesis of well-defined block copolymers. Micelles assembled from these block copolymers further exhibited regioregularity-dependent sizes and photoresponsive behavior. These findings establish endo-cyclic rROP as a previously unrecognized strategy for controlling backbone regioregularity and properties in vinyl polymers.

title: NMR Reveals Coupled Ligand and Protein Conformational Equilibria That Modulate the Affinity of MDM2-Inhibitory Peptoids
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Peptoids, atypical peptides with N-substitutions, are a promising drug modality for targeting protein–protein interactions. The binding affinity of an MDM2-inhibitory peptoid decreases by more than 100-fold upon removal of the backbone-restricting methyl groups attached to the α-carbons, although this modification alters the population of the all-trans amide-bond isomer by only 1.6-fold. This discrepancy raises the possibility that backbone flexibility affects not only ligand preorganization but also the conformational ensemble of the target protein. Here, we used NMR to examine the binding mode of the MDM2-peptoid complexes. ZZ-exchange experiments demonstrated that peptoid isomers containing cis amide bonds bind less favorably to MDM2 than the all-trans amide bond isomer. In addition, observation of the I19 δ1-methyl resonance of MDM2 in complex with the peptoids revealed that MDM2 exists in equilibrium between an open state, corresponding to the crystal structure of the MDM2-peptoid complex, and a semiclosed state, which retains partial interactions between the N-terminal region of MDM2 and the ligand-binding cleft. Increased population of the semiclosed state correlated with reduced binding affinities of the peptoids. We propose that cis-trans isomerization of the peptoid amide bonds and the conformational equilibrium of MDM2 within the peptoid complex synergistically contribute to the more than 100-fold decrease in binding affinity. These results identify coupled ligand and protein conformational equilibria as determinants of binding affinity and suggest conformational-plasticity control as a potential design principle for oligomeric ligands targeting protein–protein interactions.

title: Construction of benzochalcogenaboroles via single-atom editing of boracycles
abstract: Benzoxaborole is arguably the most important boron-based pharmacophore. Since Torssell's 1957 synthesis, hundreds of benzoxaborole derivatives have emerged, including US Food and Drug Administration-approved tavaborole and crisaborole. However, while peripheral modifications are well studied, synthetic challenges leave isoelectronic core modification less explored, despite its potential to enhance potency and reveal unexplored functions. Here we report a challenging ring expansion of benzoboretenes with elemental chalcogens, where benzoboretenes act as a 'diradical reservoir'. This synthetic protocol provides a versatile and modular platform for accessing three previously inaccessible classes of benzochalcogenaborole skeletons, in which the oxygen atom of the benzoxaborole core is formally replaced with Se, S or SO2. Preliminary biological evaluation reveals that this 'O-to-S' modification confers potent ferroptosis-inhibitory activity. Furthermore, its excellent functional group compatibility enables structure-activity optimization, leading to a 20-fold increase in cellular potency. This research not only expands the chemical space of boron-containing pharmacophores via single-atom ring expansion but also exemplifies how skeletal editing can unlock biological activities.
